author: Ismail Abukar
title: Somalia: A Government With One Foot Out the Door
content:
Somalia’s foreign passport crackdown reveals a governance crisis hiding in plain sight


On the afternoon of June 24, 2026, Somalia’s Second Deputy Prime Minister, Jibril Abdirashid Haji,

arrived at Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport

 aboard a flight from Mogadishu. Kenyan immigration officers stopped him at the gate. According to multiple reports, his Kenyan passport had been fraudulently obtained. He was deported back to Mogadishu — back to the country he was supposed to be governing.


The incident was not isolated. On July 26,

State Minister at the Presidency Abshir Bukhaari — a former First Deputy Speaker of Somalia’s Senate — was also denied entry at the same airport

 after immigration officials raised questions about his travel documents. He was placed on a return flight to Mogadishu. Neither the Kenyan nor the Somali government has officially confirmed the reasons behind the incident. Somalia’s Foreign Ministry summoned Kenya’s ambassador for consultations the following day.


Six weeks after the first deportation, Jibril became the first senior official to publicly comply with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s July ultimatum

ordering all cabinet ministers to surrender their foreign passports or resign

.

Multiple sources report that a wave of cabinet ministers is now finalising similar arrangements

. The crackdown is real. But it still does not reach the deeper layers of Somalia’s governing class — the advisors, the technical staff, the parliamentary majority — where the foreign passport has functioned not as a travel document but as a structural instrument of governance, and of exit.


The geography of power


When senior officials want to meet with traditional community leaders, they do not travel to the elders’ homes. They summon the elders to their hotels — clustered, almost without exception, near the airport.


‘They do not go to the neighbourhoods to see how civilians live their lives day by day,’ one employee at a Mogadishu ministry told me, speaking on condition of anonymity. ‘They only come to town after midnight, when the streets are half empty — and even then they have a lot of military guards. They are normally between Villa Somalia and the airport area.’


A second ministry employee described something more troubling. According to this source, state ministers and deputy ministers who hold dual citizenship do not come to the ministry at all — official stamps, documents, and administrative tools have been relocated to their airport hotels. ‘Only a secretary is at the ministry office,’ this second source said. ‘She is there to oversee the daily operations — who comes, who goes in the ministry building.’ The function of the state, in other words, has relocated to a departure lounge.


Décalé airport departure lounge, Mogadishu.


In December 2022,

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud publicly acknowledged

 that the government’s own biometric attendance system showed only 1,500 of more than 5,000 registered civil servants present at their offices. The remaining 3,500 — seventy percent of the civil service payroll — were drawing salaries without showing up. He called them ghost workers. The reaction from ordinary Somalis was outrage. The reaction from the political class was silence. ‘They have nothing tying them to Somalia besides the government title,’ one elder told me. ‘And the day that title ends, they are on the first flight out — with a lot of money made during their tenure.’


The scale of the problem


The foreign passport is not a peripheral feature of Somalia’s governing class. It is a defining one.

According to Wakiil

, the independent parliamentary accountability initiative, 105 out of 275 Federal Parliament members — 38 percent — held foreign passports in the 10th Parliament in 2017. Many of those same MPs continue to serve. In the Upper House, 20 out of 54 Senators are returned diaspora. From 2000 until 2022, every Prime Minister appointed across Somalia’s transitional and federal governments is reported to have held dual citizenship from a Western country — Canadian, Norwegian, Swedish. The current Prime Minister, Hamza Abdi Barre, holds no Western passport, and represents the first documented exception to an otherwise unbroken pattern.


Within Mogadishu’s political community, factions are informally known by the Western cities where members spent their years of exile: the ‘American Camp,’ the ‘Norwegian Colony,’ the ‘Canadian Corner.’ These are not jokes. They …

author: Abahlali_3
title: This August we honour the women of South Africa
content:
11 August 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

This August we honour the women of South Africa

This August, in women’s month, we speak of the comrades who are mothers, daughters, sisters and grandmothers, comrades who wake up every morning in the shack settlements and carry the weight of a country that has forgotten them.

We honour the women who keep their families going under conditions of brutal impoverishment and the women who resist oppression. We honour the women in our movement.

But this is not a month of celebration.

No woman is fully free in South Africa. All women are at risk of violence. Impoverished women remain profoundly oppressed.

There is no celebration when women continue to live under very dangerous conditions.

There is no celebration when a woman must walk to a communal tap after dark and risk rape or attack.

There is no celebration when there is no electricity, no running water, no toilets, and no safety for children.

There is no celebration when a woman does not know if her home will be standing tomorrow because of evictions, fires, or political violence.

For millions of impoverished women in shacks, tin houses and backyards, every day is a fight for survival.

To celebrate while all this is true is to lie.

This August we honour all the women of our movement who refused to accept poverty as fate.

We honour Nqobile Nzuza who was murdered by a police officer on a road blockade in Cato Crest on 30 September 2013. She was seventeen years old and doing her matric. She joined the road blockade in protest against the brutal attacks on the Marikana Land Occupation in Cato Manor by the eThekwini Municipality. She was committed to the struggle for land.

We honour Comrade Thuli Ndlovu, a leader of Abahlali baseMjondolo in KwaNdengezi. She fought for land, for housing, and for the dignity of her community. She was assassinated on 27 September 2014 for confronting oppression.

We honour Comrade Nokuthula Mabaso, a leader of eKhenana Commune and of the Abahlali Women’s League. She was a mother, an organiser, and a builder of a community that fed itself and governed itself. She was assassinated on 5 May 2022 while her community was under attack. She knew that poor people must seize the right to land and to live with dignity.

Our brave comrades refused oppression and insisted on land and dignity. Thuli and Nokuthula were leaders.

We also honour other women who have given their lives in the struggle for justice.

Fikile Ntshangase was a leading member of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) which opposed the destruction of people’s land and homes by coal mining. She was assassinated on 22 October 2020.

Babita Deokaran was an honest civil servant and a whistleblower in the Gauteng Department of Health. She exposed corruption and the theft of public money meant for the public hospitals and clinics that serve the poor. She was assassinated in 2021 for refusing to look away as powerful and dangerous men looted the healthcare system.

We have no interest in politicians who come with speeches and flowers and say nothing about the oppression we live today and nothing about our leaders who have given their lives in the struggle against this oppression.

1.⁠ ⁠Secure access to land and decent housing so no woman sleeps in fear of eviction or fire. 2.⁠ Access to basic services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and safe public lighting in every settlement. 3.⁠ ⁠An end to political killings and intimidation of women organisers. 4.⁠ ⁠An end to gender-based violence in homes, streets, schools and communities. 5.⁠ ⁠Decent work, healthcare and education so women are not forced to choose between feeding their children and their own health. 6. Reproductive healthcare and contraception available without humiliation or delay. 7. A livable guaranteed income in recognition of the unpaid care work that holds families and communities together. 8. Decisive action to reduce food prices on essential items. 9. An end to attempts to turn poor women against migrant and refugee women, since the enemy is landlessness, unemployment and state neglect, not our neighbours. 10.⁠ ⁠Accountability for the killings of Nqobile, Thuli, Nokuthula, Fikile, Babita and all the other murdered and assassinated women activists whose cases were closed and forgotten.

Poor women are not asking to be celebrated. We are demanding to be safe, to be housed, to be heard, to be alive.

Until that happens, August …

author: Kalundi Serumaga
title: US-Iran Ceasefire: America is at a Crossroads
content:
The agreement (called a “Memorandum of Understanding”) signed between the United States and Iran in mid-June needs careful study in order to understand its real implications for the future of the Middle East, the United States, and the global economy that rests on the relationship between the two.


Basically, America accepted that Iran would control the global oil choke point that is the Strait of Hormuz, that the country would be compensated for all the damage caused by American and Israeli bombs and other military action over the last several months, and that it would be allowed to resume global trading in oil and have its assets that are currently frozen in the West returned to it. In exchange, Iran agreed to not pursue a nuclear military programme (which is theologically banned in Iran anyway), and to allow a temporary free passage through the Strait of Hormuz so as  to clear the shipping backlog.


The situation remains fluid. The agreement began to fall apart almost immediately, with the American side (that is, the USA being held responsible for the actions of Israel) failing to control itself on the battlefields and also making unnecessary threats.


This is a very old American habit. A settler mindset. The collection of surviving indigenous Native American communities has this in their cultural memory. Of the nearly four hundred treaties the arriving white settler-state signed with the “Native Americans” between 1778 and 1871, not one was ever fully honoured. Attacks and genocide were what came instead.   


In this case, the American side first tried to wriggle out of the Iranian agreement by changing facts on the ground. They achieved a “side quest” of getting Lebanon’s weak government to come to its own agreement with the invading Israelis the substance of which is to accept the fact of the Israeli military occupation of southern Lebanon, and to oblige the Lebanese government to disarm the Iranian-allied Hezbollah, which is basically the armed resistance embedded among the communities of south Lebanon, and which has been an enormous obstacle to Israeli ambitions there.


This move is aimed directly at undermining that part of the American-Iranian MoU that obliged the Americans to make their friend Israel withdraw militarily from Lebanon.


But such gambits are actually the secondary issue. What really matters is the fact that America found itself in a position where it had to agree to such terms, even for twenty-four hours, and also, therefore, had to relate to a Middle Eastern country as a complete equal.


American president Donald Trump even dejectedly admitted in a press conference shortly thereafter that there was nothing else his country could have done except agree to such terms. Trump even went as far as acknowledging Iran’s right to a nuclear energy programme, its right to self-defence and, therefore, to a missile programme.


The Middle East, as the centre of the world’s new energy source, emerged as the Jewel in the Crown of the emerging American global empire beginning in 1946, following the exhaustion of the global Western European powers from too much war.


America became exceptionally wealthy partly through making its currency the basis of world savings and then backing it up twenty years later as the compulsory currency for trade in oil. This led to financial irresponsibility. Over the decades, America began issuing more and more dollars as if they were as valuable as the original ones.


A situation emerged whereby the amount of dollars in use globally now far exceeds the actual physical value of the American economy that is supposed to back them up. This gap can be understood in figures. The public debt of the United States stands at a record thirty-one trillion dollars. This represents an over 100 per cent debt-to-GDP ratio and attracts an annual interest bill of about one billion dollars.


If this situation is not resolved, or seen to be being resolved, then a time will come when global money markets will lose faith in the United States’ stock market, treasury bills and, ultimately, even the dollar itself as a currency. Investment money will migrate to other currency marketsand other forms of wealth.


As original Wailer Peter Tosh prophesized:


“The day the dollar die

Things are gonna be better

The day the dollar die

No more corruption

The day the dollar die

People will respect each other

The day the dollar die..


This situation is bad for the ordinary American too …

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Negotiations with security officials end Warraq residents’ sit-in for better services
content:
Residents of Warraq Island suspended on Monday a sit-in they had convened, blocking the supply of building materials to a government construction project on the island, to demand access to their own materials and to demand the improvement of basic services, according to residents of the island who spoke to Mada Masr.


They said they agreed to suspend the sit-in after negotiations with security officials who promised to accede to their demands. 


The protest came a week after clashes with security forces resumed over authorities’ restrictions on the delivery of construction materials from the city, part of a policy aimed at emptying the island of its residents to make way for a development project that would turn it into a “new city.”


Families living on the Nile island began their sit-in on Sunday outside the arrival point for the ferry that carries vehicles transporting building materials for the government’s construction project on the island.


“We’re staying here until the government comes to hear our demands,” one resident told Mada Masr before the sit-in was suspended. “We’re for development, but don’t make things harder for us,” they said, pointing to how residents want to ensure that development does not come at the expense of their lives and daily needs. 


A second resident said the sit-in had initially been planned to continue until the end of the week, with protestors scheduled to meet on Friday to discuss their next steps. According to the resident, they temporarily suspended the protest after Monday’s negotiations with security officials while they waited for a response to their demands.


A third resident summed up the urgent demands as including: the restoration of the work of sewage pumping trucks, as the island’s sewage tanks are full; the removal of the security barriers installed at the island’s two entrances at the Qolaly and Shubra ferry crossings and replacing them with basic inspection procedures; and the repair of street lighting services. 


Families are also calling for improving healthcare services, according to the third resident, including the provision of a doctor at the island’s hospital. Residents currently have to leave Warraq for emergency and serious medical treatment after the state

closed

the local health unit in 2021 under the pretext of conducting maintenance.


The third resident described these as simple and immediate demands that the state could easily meet as a gesture of “good faith.” Responding to the demands, they said, would be seen as a first step toward engaging with residents, rather than continuing to adopt pressure policies against them and would signal to the residents that the state is prepared to enter into serious talks about conditions under which they can maintain their right to continue living on the island. That would require making everyday life easier, including allowing residents to build and to bring in vehicles carrying construction materials. Another

key demand,

 they said, is for a state representative to engage with residents to discuss their situation and the island’s future.


Clashes broke out between security forces and dozens of the island’s residents near the Qolaly ferry crossing last week after a security officer assaulted a boy in an attempt to prevent him from bringing building materials over from the city, according to accounts

published

 online by several residents. The clashes lasted for several consecutive days, with three protestors arrested and later released. 


The third resident referred to conditions on the island as a “siege” that has lasted for nine years, with heightened security measures such as checkpoints at the island’s entrances, as security forces have shut down three of the five ferries that used to tie the Nile island to the rest of the city.


Residents started

organizing

 to oppose the government’s plan to expel them from their homes in 2017 and have continued to do so after the government clarified in the intervening years its plans to develop the island and the issuance of a series of expropriation decisions. 


Warraq residents have complained of tighter restrictions on the delivery of building materials for around a month, considering the development a form of pressure intended to force them to leave their homes and accept the compensation they are being offered by the government as part of the development project on the island and the expropriation decisions that come with it. 


Clashes, which flare …

author: William Shoki
title: On Safari
content:
Ever since the

World Cup

 concluded with Spain’s emphatic triumph over universally loathed Argentina (at least it felt this way), it has no longer felt like everyone is looking in the same direction at the same time. For a month and a bit, football’s biggest stage gave us one of the last remaining experiences of shared, global time. Not global justice, not global equality — the tournament is in many ways a monument to their absence — but a crude, synchronized schedule. Games at set hours, short-lived solidarities, the impression, however false, that the world is briefly doing something together, undergoing a collective experience.

Once that all ends, you’re plunged back into a social temporality and news cycle that moves at lightning speed and adjusting back is disorienting. It didn’t help that I had to deal with a debilitating case of

cyclosporiasis

 (in an ill-fated decision, I tried some Taco Bell for the first time the day before my return flight back to South Africa, and getting a food-borne illness felt like an appropriate parting gift from a United States in decline). In the weeks since the World Cup, I found myself in a kind of fog I at first attributed to being exhausted from a busy year coupled with bouts of illness, but which, as I return to relatively decent health, I recognize as a familiar feeling, one that has typified contemporary experience for as long as I can remember.

There’s a book by the Polish sociologist Zygmunt Bauman which I think is underrated, and does better at capturing the texture of our epoch than many other attempts (do we live in late capitalism, surveillance capitalism, the burnout society, post-modernity, etc etc.). It’s called

Liquid Modernity

, and Bauman’s straightforward argument is that the defining feature of contemporary society is no longer the construction of stable institutions, identities, and social relationships, but their constant dissolution. Where the “solid” phase of modernity sought to build enduring structures — stable careers, lifelong marriages, nation-states, political parties, class identities, and fixed moral frameworks — our present condition is “liquid”: forms no longer retain their shape for long enough to organize human life. The contradictory result of this is that even though in many important respects, individuals have unprecedented freedom (at least compared to any other point in human history), it’s coupled with chronic insecurity and the burden of constantly having to remake ourselves.

One of his most evocative concepts is the notion of pointillist time, which is “more prominent for its inconsistency and lack of cohesion than for its elements of continuity and consistency.” Time under liquid modernity is fragmented and disconnected, and rather than unfolding as a series of events with some relationship to each other, it is rather a series of “eternal instants.” It’s not hard work to see how this characterizes so much of algorithm-dominated society in general, and our media consumption in particular. If it wasn’t hard enough figuring out what producing any meaningful “content” takes in the attention economy, it was dismaying for me to recently learn that even new media like podcasts and video essays are themselves now being repurposed in a

“clipping economy”

 where increasingly, circulation of short clips from longer pieces is becoming the main event rather than previews.

At

Africa Is a Country

, we are very proud of our World Cup Road Trip series. Three episodes are live —

Episode 1

 on the Cabo Verdean diaspora in New England,

Episode 2

 on the affinity between Algeria and Lawrence, Kansas, and

Episode 3

 on Toronto’s Ghanaian community — with further episodes from the road currently in post-production. Although the website and our weekly newsletters remain our bread and butter, like most outlets, we are experimenting with different ways of reaching audiences, and short-form video has been one of them. The newsletter in particular functions as our most reliable direct channel to readers as social platform referrals grow less dependable. The World Cup, however, gave us a powerful on-ramp: sport brought in readers who might not otherwise arrive at a piece on visa regimes or xenophobia, and the coverage was built to convert that interest into political understanding.

What has been challenging is that discovery is now heavily platform-dependent, and the same work travels very differently depending on where it lands: our road trip …

author: ROAPE
title: The extraversion of African academic journals
content:
There is a long history of donor funding for African universities, research and publishing, going back to the colonial period, and the foundation of the International African Institute in 1926. The crises of higher education and knowledge flows of the 1980s, described by the historian of Africa Michael Crowder as a ‘book famine’, led to a plethora of donor-funded initiatives in support of African journals, book publishing and donations. New publishing NGOs were established including the International Network for the Availability of Scientific Publication and African Journals Online (AJOL). Later, other NGOs promoting access to Northern published journals included the Dutch-based Electronic Information for Libraries (EIFL) and the Research4Life (R4L) partnership funded by UN agencies and several of the major commercial publishers including the largest scientific publisher Elsevier.


Although these NGOs have increased access to online publishing, and to journals published by the commercial presses, they have not strengthened the economic sustainability of African journals. Over 25 years after the launch of these NGOs, African journals remain as dependent on donor funding as they were at inception. Digital discoverability tools, submission platforms, and publishing standards have rapidly evolved, making traditional print publishing obsolete, marginalising journals, and reinforcing knowledge hierarchies.


Dependency and extraversion


Hountondji understood dependency as a condition created by the capitalist core, colonial or metropolitan centres, over the colonial peripheries. This has underpinned the extraversion of scientific publishing and dependency on development donors. As Hountondji foresaw, the science communication system reinforces extraversion and dependency. 


Well before the promises of the internet economy and debates about digital or data colonialism, Hountondji

wrote

 that scientific infrastructure on the continent mainly served to facilitate the export of information and data, integrating the scientific legacy of the South into the intellectual production managed and controlled by the North.


The dependence of African academics on international journals and their reviewers has a well-documented negative impact on academic autonomy. Echoing Hountondji, Nyamnjoh rightly 

argues

 that the African academy continues to suffer from endemic reliance on external validation through Northern journals.


Jean-François Bayart criticised Hountondji and dependency theory for not properly historicising societies. Bayart developed the concept of extraversion in a new and different way, focusing on the political agency of African elites. He argued that in unequal environments elite actors, such as NGOs, may deliberately deploy ‘financial extraversion’ to mobilise donor aid. His work emphasises the actions of private foreign actors, or multinational companies, that capture Africa’s trade with Europe for purposes of commercial gain, exacerbating Africa’s dependence.  


The fall and rise of multinational publishers


During the late colonial period, British multinationals dominated publishing in anglophone Africa. Their presence expanded in the postcolonial period due to increased demand for educational materials in the newly independent states. Most multinational operators withdrew in the financial crisis of the 1980s as textbooks became increasingly unaffordable.


Where once Macmillan and Oxford University Press controlled textbook markets, including in apartheid South Africa, the company with the largest academic footprint today is Taylor & Francis (T&F). Exploiting the market opportunities brought about by the end of apartheid from the mid-1990s, T&F has taken over the publishing of over 70 Africa-related journals, setting up co-publishing agreements with the University of South Africa and launching many new journals.


More recently, T&F has been publishing a rapidly growing number of papers in its ‘mega’ journals modelled on those of the science publishers. Around 40% of articles published in T&F’s 

Cogent Social Sciences

 are from Africa. Many of these papers are published with open access waivers or discounts funded by its partnership with the donor-funded EIFL. T&F

reports

 that since 2020 more than 18,000 researchers have received either 50% discounts or complete fee waivers to publish in its journals.


The library at the Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar, Senegal (Wikimedia Commons, 2008)


R4L …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Senegal’s World Cup Exit: The Price of National Honor and Women’s Safety
content:
The reigning African champions were eliminated from the 2026 FIFA World Cup on 1 July, beaten 3-2 by Belgium in extra time in the Round of 32. The Lions of Teranga had gone two goals up early, lifting hopes across the country and the continent, before Belgium’s comeback sent them home. What has followed is a dramatic unfolding of events that expose the disturbing and persistent patterns beyond the Senegalese team. 


During the tournament, players were reportedly seen ordering food outside their designated hotel. The detail seemed trivial until it emerged that the team’s chef was not with the squad at all. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) initially pointed to visa problems, easy to accept given the treatment African teams and supporters have received from the United States and Canada as hosts. 


But as scrutiny mounted, a different account surfaced. More than ten days after the defeat, the federation’s general secretary, Abdoulaye Seydou Sow, appeared on the Senegalese public broadcaster RTS on

Sunday, July 12

and confirmed what social media had reported: the chef had been accused of sexual harassment by an employee recruited in the United States. Faced with the allegations, Sow said, “the federation chose to act without delay.”

 

The chef was sent home. 


“Everyone should congratulate the federation president and me because we protected Senegal’s honor and dignity,” Sow said. “We did not want to make the matter public, but once we became aware of the facts and the procedures that could follow, we acted immediately.”


Keeping him on American soil, Sow explained, might have invited intervention by US authorities. The removal was a precaution: to preserve calm in the squad and keep the matter from disrupting Senegal’s campaign. He went further, noting that the secretary general also stressed that certain behaviors that might be perceived in Senegal as mere joking can, under American law, be considered harassment. That the federation had acted with caution to avoid potential legal or media consequences that might damage the image of the team and the country. He spoke with pride of a man who believed he had guarded Senegal’s “honor and dignity”.


At no time did the official go beyond reputational handling to address safeguarding. It is a reputational one. The complainant is entirely absent from the account: we are not told whether an investigation was opened, whether she was supported, or what became of her. The chef was moved out of American jurisdiction, and the country wasn’t told if he was still in a position of authority. The federation solved exposure, not harm.


Sexual harassment at the global stage


His words sparked immediate anger online, and rightly so. In distinguishing Senegalese joking from American law, he made consent a matter of geography. His words echo what we live every day. Ask any Senegalese woman, and she will give you an inventory: the sexist joke, the vulgar remark, the hand that lands on you in a crowded place, the man who does not ask because he has never had to. This is what we are told is culture. Men joke, men pat, men say things, and nothing about it is deemed inappropriate. 


The statement is as true as it is unflinching. It says out loud what is usually left implicit, and, in doing so, stamps society’s approval on it. What shocks is the casualness: that a man at that level would relay it to the nation as though we should carry on and accept it. To the man at the top of Senegalese football, he was standing up for his buddies and the nation’s collective pride, weighing both against a woman’s safety. He did not think to denounce sexual misconduct at all.


Sexual harassment violates human rights, yet the federation’s account makes no reference to the codes that bind it. Under


FIFA rules

, sexual abuse, harassment and exploitation are not subject to any limitation period, an acknowledgement that such cases often surface years later. So removing the alleged perpetrator from the scene doesn’t necessarily resolve the case. FIFA’s framework also requires member associations to appoint a safeguarding officer and maintain reporting channels for anyone working with, in, or around them. The FSF has not said whether it has either. Evading accountability in the name of the nation is the same instinct that drives the corruption and mismanagement dogging the FSF through this tournament.

author: Precious Obiabunmo
title: ‘I wanted to be treated with dignity’: Why Nigerian women are returning to traditional birth attendants
content:
Illustration Description:

A stylized illustration shows two adults (an elderly midwife and a young nurse) gently passing a newborn baby from one pair of hands to another. The baby lies on its back wrapped in a light cloth, with only the adults’ arms and parts of their bodies visible.


Bukola Osoba had prepared herself for the pain of labour. What she had not prepared for was the noise.


The ward was overcrowded, the air thick and stifling. Nurses moved between beds with the attitude of people who had long stopped seeing patients as people owed compassion. When she called out during a contraction, nobody came. When someone finally did, they spoke to her in a clipped, impatient tone. She left that hospital having delivered her  child and feeling, somehow, that something had been taken from her.  


“They’re very nonchalant,” she says.”That was why I opted for traditional birth care.”


Osoba is not alone in that conclusion. Across Nigeria, a quiet but growing number of women are turning away from the formal health system, reaching instead toward something older: herbalists, elder mothers and community midwives whose knowledge was passed down not in lecture theatres but through observation, repetition and inheritance. Women who, for generations before colonisation, held birth as their domain.


For Ugwuanyi Akubuenyi, the decision stemmed from both conviction and disillusionment in modern practice. She simply believed, deeply, that there was another way – one rooted in how her people had always lived. 


“I sat down one day asking myself how our ancient women gave birth without the help of orthodox medication and hospital,” she says. “I just concluded I was going to follow the same procedure when I get pregnant.”


It is a conclusion that carries weight in a country where the stakes of childbirth could not be higher.


Nigeria is the world’s most dangerous nation in which to give birth. According to the

 most recent UN estimates

, compiled from 2023 figures, one in every 100 women dies in labour or in the days that follow. That same year, Nigeria accounted for 29 per cent of all maternal deaths worldwide – an estimated 75,000 women, one every seven minutes.


Against that backdrop, the turn towards traditional birth care is not without controversy.

Health authorities

 have identified it as one of the factors contributing to the country’s catastrophic mortality figures. The tension, then, is real and uncomfortable: how do you reconcile the warmth and dignity women describe finding in ancestral practice with the cold arithmetic of who is dying, and why?


Aderonke Abdul, a narrative strategist and researcher who has herself experienced the failures of Nigeria’s maternal healthcare system, both public and private, has spent considerable time sitting with that contradiction in her research,

Herbal Wombs, Modern Medicine

.


“Before modern medicine entered what we now call Nigeria, birthing was not an isolated medical event,” she explains. “It was a deeply communal, spiritual and embodied process. Care was held by experienced women: midwives, elder mothers, herbalists. They understood the rhythms of the body through observation, repetition, and inheritance. Birth happened at home, in familiar spaces, with hands that had done this work many times before.”


Before colonisation fragmented it, childbirth was understood as continuous and holistic. Care stretched from prenatal preparation through to postpartum recovery, attending equally to body, mind and spirit. Women were given herbs to strengthen the womb, guided through emotional and spiritual fortification, supported during labour with massages, chants and positioning techniques, then nurtured afterward with hot baths, abdominal binding, and nutrient-rich soups. At the centre of it all was community: midwives, doulas, herbalists, and daughters learning through proximity and shared knowledge across generations.


Colonisation reframed all of that as superstition.


Nkiruka Epechwao carries both worlds in her. A traditional herbalist and midwife from a lineage of healers, she runs her own maternal health clinic while holding modern certification and having previously worked inside the formal healthcare system. 


“Most midwives and doctors in the hospital work carnally. And most of them are impatient,” she says. 


The impatience, she argues, has consequences that show up on the operating table. 


“Some doctors and nurses will shout at the patients and the blood …

author: Sondes Zarrouki
title: Liberté d’expression en Tunisie : Recul alarmant sous le joug du décret 54 et de l’article 86
content:
Depuis la révolution de 2011, la Tunisie était saluée comme un modèle de transition démocratique dans le monde arabe, avec une Constitution de 2014 qui consacrait la liberté d’expression, la séparation des pouvoirs et un pluralisme politique. Mais à partir de 2021, avec le coup de force de Kais Saied (dissolution du Parlement, mainmise sur le judiciaire…), ce paysage a connu un net recul. Le président a fait adopter une nouvelle Constitution en 2022, qui renforce considérablement les pouvoirs exécutifs au détriment des contre-pouvoirs. Parallèlement, il a promulgué par décret-loi le décret n° 2022-54, qui remplace et durcit les dispositions protectrices du décret 115 de 2011 sur la liberté de la presse, de l’impression et de l’édition.
Le décret 54 : une arme à double tranchant contre la critique
Ce texte, officiellement destiné à combattre les infractions liées aux systèmes d’information et de communication, a rapidement été détourné de son objectif affiché. En remplaçant le décret 115, qui avait aboli les peines de prison pour diffamation et protégé les sources journalistiques, le décret 54 introduit des sanctions plus lourdes et des définitions plus vagues. Son article 24 punit de cinq ans de prison et d’une amende de 50 000 dinars la diffusion de “fausses nouvelles”, rumeurs ou données falsifiées portant atteinte aux droits d’autrui, à la sûreté publique ou semant la terreur. Les peines sont doublées si la cible est un fonctionnaire.
Le texte impose par ailleurs aux opérateurs de télécommunications l’obligation de conserver systématiquement, pendant au moins deux ans, les données permettant d’identifier leurs utilisateurs. Une disposition que Human Rights Watch juge attentatoire au droit à la vie privée, indépendamment même de son usage répressif contre la liberté d’expression.
Des organisations comme Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Reporters sans frontières (RSF) et le Syndicat national des journalistes tunisiens (SNJT) dénoncent un outil devenu, dans la pratique, un instrument de répression incompatible avec les standards internationaux. Selon le SNJT, plus de 60 journalistes, avocats et opposants politiques ont fait l’objet de poursuites judiciaires en vertu de ce décret depuis son entrée en vigueur fin 2022. Un décompte plus récent, centré sur les seuls professionnels des médias, recense 24 cas judiciaires engagés en vertu du décret 54, dont 21 initiés par des institutions officielles, parmi elles, sept directement à l’initiative du ministère public. Le décret criminalise ainsi l’expression critique et crée un climat d’autocensure généralisée : une simple publication Facebook peut, en théorie comme en pratique, entraîner plusieurs années de prison.
L’article 86 du code des télécommunications : Un outil complémentaire
Cet article, souvent utilisé en tandem avec le décret 54, punit d’un à deux ans de prison quiconque “sciemment nuit aux tiers ou perturbe leur quiétude“ via les réseaux publics de télécommunications. Sa formulation, tout aussi imprécise que celle du décret 54, élargit l’arsenal juridique contre les publications en ligne jugées gênantes par les autorités ou par des particuliers disposant de relais institutionnels.
Des prisonniers politiques et des arrestations qui s’intensifient
La répression touche l’opposition, la société civile et les médias, avec une trajectoire clairement ascendante depuis 2023. Human Rights Watch et Amnesty International recensaient plus de 40 personnes en détention arbitraire en mai 2024. Ce chiffre est passé à plus de 50 en janvier 2025, selon le rapport mondial 2025 de HRW.
Le rapport “Tous des Comploteurs“, publié en avril 2025, documente en détail 22 cas de personnes incarcérées sur la base d’accusations abusives, allant de la diffusion de fausses nouvelles au terrorisme, dont au moins 14 risqueraient la peine capitale si elles étaient reconnues coupables.
Parmi les affaires emblématiques : la condamnation de l’avocate et commentatrice Sonia Dahmani, arrêtée en mai 2024 puis condamnée à plusieurs reprises pour des propos tenus dans des émissions. Celle des journalistes Borhen Bsaies et Mourad Zeghidi, condamnés à un an de prison (réduit à huit mois) pour des déclarations en vertu du décret 54 ou encore celle de Abir Moussi, présidente du Parti destourien libre, condamnée à deux ans de prison pour avoir diffusé de “fausses nouvelles“ sur l’instance électorale.
Des procès de masse et des accusations de “complot“ ou de terrorisme complètent ce tableau, souvent …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: South Africans protest against xenophobia
content:
Thousands took to the streets of Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg on Friday calling for an end to the xenophobic violence that is fanned by anti-immigrant groups. Led by Operation Ubuntu and Siyafana Sonke Campaign, and backed by over 80 civil society organisations, the protesters delivered a memorandum of demands to the South African Police Services and various government departments.


The first stop for the Cape Town protest was at the Cape Town Central Police Station where the recently appointed provincial police commissioner, Lt Gen Sizakhele Dyantyi. received the memorandum. The protesters called for an end to the xenophobia perpetrated by the police, and for the arrest and prosecution of March & March ringleaders.


“Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, Nkosikhona Ndabandaba (Phakel’umthakathi), Ngizwe Mchunu have to be arrested and prosecuted for hate speech, inciting violence, and in Phakel’umthakathi’s case, assaulting migrants. Their actions have led to the forced removal of 160,000 people, our largest forced removal ever. The state has protected them before and since June 30, letting them act with impunity, which has emboldened vigilante groups,” said Shaheed Mohamed, secretary of the Worker International Vanguard League.


Outside parliament in Cape Town, protesters handed over a memorandum of demands to representatives from the departments of Human Settlement, Home Affairs, and Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (Cogta), as well as the Presidency.


They demanded that the Department of Human Settlement work with social justice and community structures to come up with a fresh bill on land and housing that is informed by community experiences and supported by existing research. In June, land and housing organisations

rejected the Prevention of Illegal Eviction Amendment Bill

and called on the government to deal with the housing crisis instead.


The memorandum stated that Cogta should implement disaster relief in all the areas where migrants are displaced in order to provide humanitarian relief and that there should be negotiation and reintegration as per the South African report on migration of 2023.


From Home Affairs, they demanded that the White Paper on Citizenship and Immigration be halted as some sections are deemed unconstitutional. For instance, the white paper proposes that asylum seekers are not by right entitled to a fair hearing, which is contrary to the Refugee Convention. “Enact an immediate 2-year moratorium on expulsions (voluntary repatriations) in order to allow African migrants to obtain their documents. Resolve the national identity documentation backlog, which has left an estimated 4-million South Africans without IDs, and address the backlog of expired or unprocessed migrant documentation by providing documentation. End mass expulsions and the prevailing climate of fear around documentation, which is functioning like a new dompas,” reads the memorandum.


The protesters called for an end to the xenophobic violence and for the state to be accountable for its actions.


Congolese Civil Society of South Africa (CCSSA) chairperson, Isaiah Mumbilo called for African unity against xenophobia as divisions are in the interest of colonisers and corporations. “Instead of talking about how to protect our natural and mineral resources that we have in the continent, we are prioritising hate of each other in the form of xenophobia,” he said.


The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has faced war and conflict resulting in an estimated 6-million deaths since 1996, a crisis that is driven by the

violent control and exploitation of lucrative rare minerals and natural resources

.


Activist and feminist, Takwana Maema said that migration is a tool that colonialists and capitalists have always used to pull down black bodies, and take control of land and resources. “We need not be taken into making false choices; we need to reject false choices! We need to unite, we need to look at the economic systems and see that these systems continue to perpetuate the fact that Africa continues to stay at the bottom,” she said.


Amadoda Aqotho, a men’s movement based in Khayelitsha, said that they joined the anti-xenophobia protest because the current xenophobic protests and violence scapegoats African migrants and excuses government and those in power. “We joined our African brothers and sisters because we understand that we should not be fighting each other as those in government and in power benefit …

author: Hassan Ali Sanhori
title: A Century of Agricultural Investment in Sudan: Why Has Development Failed?
content:
This article is translated and adapted from an Arabic article published in

Sudanese Online

. The ideas reflect arguments presented by the author in his

book

 on agriculture in Sudan.


For decades, Sudan has been described as one of Africa’s countries with the greatest agricultural potential. Its vast arable land, diverse climatic zones, water resources, and livestock wealth have repeatedly led policymakers to portray it as a potential “breadbasket” for Africa and the Arab world.


However, a persistent paradox remains: despite more than a century of agricultural investment, Sudan has failed to transform agriculture into a driver of inclusive development or a foundation for political and social stability. Rural Sudan has grown poorer and more vulnerable, while areas that should have been sources of food security and prosperity have become centers of conflict and of displacement.


Today, after the war that began on April 15, 2023, this paradox is clearer than ever before. The war did not destroy the thriving agricultural sector. Rather, it exposed the limits of an investment model that failed to deliver balanced development, strengthen food security, or build peace over many decades.


This raises a fundamental question: if Sudan has the resources and investment has continued, why has its rural population remained poor and vulnerable, with limited access to services, while the countryside has become the main theatre of many of the country’s armed conflicts?


The answer lies in the fact that Sudan’s crisis has never been simply a crisis of resources or financing. This is a crisis in the agricultural investment model itself.


Since the establishment of the Gezira Scheme in the 1920s, followed by the New Halfa, Rahad, and Suki schemes, the expansion of mechanized rain-fed agriculture, and programmes supported by international institutions after independence, agricultural investment has generally been measured by the number of cultivated hectares, the volume of production, or the value of exports.


More fundamental questions have largely been excluded from the debate: who benefits from investment? Where is the investment directed? Does it address the roots of marginalisation? Does it build local institutions and sustainable markets?


Some of these projects succeeded in increasing production during specific periods. However, they did not produce a structural transformation of the rural economy, narrow the gap between the center and peripheries, or establish integrated agricultural markets capable of creating decent employment and improving living standards.


Indeed, some agricultural policies indirectly deepened regional inequalities and reinforced the sense of marginalization, which later became one of the drivers of conflict in Sudan.


This problem is particularly evident when comparing different investment patterns. Large irrigated schemes receive a disproportionate share of public financing, infrastructure, and research and extension services. In contrast, traditional rain-fed agriculture, on which millions of farmers and pastoralists in Darfur, Kordofan, Blue Nile, and large parts of eastern Sudan depend, remained outside national planning priorities for decades.


Simultaneously, mechanised rain-fed agriculture expanded at the expense of forests, grazing lands, and pastoral routes. This has contributed to growing disputes over land and natural resources.


The livestock sector did not perform much better. Despite their major contribution to exports and rural livelihoods, investment in veterinary services, infrastructure, markets, and value chains remains limited. This weakened one of the sectors with the greatest potential to support balanced and geographically inclusive developments.


Structural consequences


Historical agricultural investment policies have produced consequences that go far beyond economic indicators. They have affected Sudan’s social fabric, political relations, and environmental systems. These policies were not merely technical or economic decisions; they reflected structural and ideological biases in how development was conceived and implemented.


Poverty


The extractive and centralized investment model generates sharp economic inequalities. According to the figures cited in this analysis, approximately 60 percent of financing was directed towards large irrigated schemes in the central regions, 30 percent towards large-scale mechanized rain-fed agriculture, and only 10 percent …

author: Mark Blackburn
title: Yukon committee calls for urgent action following child welfare audit
content:
A non-partisan committee of Yukon MLAs says it’s “not convinced” the Department of Health and Social Services has sufficiently considered recommendations from a scathing Auditor General’s report on its Child and Family Services branch – and is calling for quick action to address ongoing concerns.


The statement stems from a

new report

 released by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts – made up of MLAs from the territory’s three parties – which includes 20 recommendations to bolster follow-up and accountability following a March 2026 audit.


The report outlines seven “critical areas” that it says require further attention, including group home policies; staff training; staffing shortages; critical incident reporting; challenges in smaller communities; data collection; and monitoring outcomes.


Its recommendations include departmental updates on the targeted hiring of First Nation social workers, staffing levels and critical incidents, as well as a timeline for updating group home policies.


The committee also wants the department to update its case management system to “clearly reflect and make accessible whether caregivers of children currently in care were themselves in government care, attended residential schools, or have a history of abuse.”


It further calls on the department to “make efforts” to involve children, families and caregivers so their perspectives and experiences are meaningfully incorporated.


The March 2026 audit paints a grim picture of child welfare in the territory.


Deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes

said at the time of the audit’s release

 that the Yukon government was falling short in protecting the safety and well-being of vulnerable children and families, especially Indigenous children.


The report, which reviewed records from late 2022 to March 31, 2025, highlighted issues that Hayes called “concerning.”


The audit found the department failed to evaluate the need for protective intervention within the mandated 24-hour window in 37 per cent of child harm allegations. In cases where assessments identified the need for further investigation, the department did not complete investigations within the required 30 days in 41 per cent of cases it reviewed.


It further highlighted systemic gaps in cases involving home screening before children could be placed with extended family or in foster homes. It noted criminal record checks were not completed for all adults in extended family homes in 22 per cent of the cases it reviewed.


The Council of Yukon First Nations told APTN News at the time that 98 per cent of children in care in the territory are Indigenous.


Read More:


Audit finds ‘serious gaps’ in Yukon’s child welfare system 


The audit’s recommendations include improving compliance monitoring, reviewing staffing levels and collaborating with Indigenous partners to complete cultural plans for Indigenous children in care – all of which the government has accepted.


The committee, which is mandated to examine the administration of public programs and services, including recommendations made by the Auditor General, held a public hearing on the matter in May.


“The Public Accounts Committee expects to see further progress on addressing the issues highlighted by the Auditor General’s report,” the committee said, noting there could be more public hearings in the future.


A press release states the report will be tabled in the legislature when it sits this fall.


With files from Sara Connors

Yukon committee calls for urgent action following child welfare audit

APTN News

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Fire destroys former federal day school building in Taloyoak
content:
Flames fully engulfed an unused building in Taloyoak that once served as a federal day school Saturday morning, sending plumes of smoke into the community as volunteer firefighters battled the blaze. 


Taloyoak firefighters work to contain a blaze at a former federal day school and craft shop Saturday.  (Photo by Bruce Holwell/Special to Nunatsiaq News)


The fire was reported to the RCMP at about 9 a.m. on Aug. 8, Cpl. Ashley Daley said in an email.


Ten volunteer firefighters arrived within five minutes and used two water trucks to fight the blaze, fire chief Steve Aqqaq said in an interview Tuesday.


“We were at the fire scene for about eight hours and had to return a couple times as it rekindled,” Aqqaq said.


Firefighters briefly entered the building but could only stay inside for 10 seconds because of the fire’s intensity, he said. East winds worsened the circumstances.


At one point, firefighters heard popping sounds. They exited the building and said that ammunition was stored inside.

For their own safety, the crew had to back away and allow the fire to burn before they continued, Aqqaq said. It’s unclear whose ammunition was stored.


While the building that caught fire was completely destroyed, its neighbours remain standing, as firefighters were able to keep them from catching, Aqqaq said.


No injuries or evacuations were reported, Daley said.


The building had been used as a federal day school between November 1958 and April 1969, according to indiandayschools.org. Aqqaq said it later housed a craft shop but had been boarded up for “many, many years.”


The cause of the fire remains under investigation, Daley said.

author: C4SS
title: Insureksi atau Revolusi?
content:
Saul Newman

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

Insurrection

 or Revolution?

”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Pada saat narasi besar tentang Revolusi yang kita warisi dari modernitas dan diskursus rasionalis Pencerahan hampir runtuh, apa alternatif yang ada untuk mengonseptualisasikan transformasi radikal? Meski tidak adanya kelas atau gerakan revolusioner yang terorganisir, pada saat yang sama kaum kiri tidak mampu berpikir melampaui gagasan emansipasi revolusioner. Kegagalan imajinasi radikal inilah yang mungkin menjadi alasan kebuntuan politik yang dihadapi kaum kiri saat ini.


Karena tidak mampu menciptakan perubahan yang bermakna, kaum kiri malah terjebak dalam “perang budaya” dan terlibat dalam politik identitas melawan kaum kanan yang jauh lebih terampil memainkan permainan ini. Dogmatisme puritan dan semangat keagamaan yang mengiringi perdebatan tanpa akhir tentang identitas gender, ras, inklusi kaum marginal, dan sebagainya menunjukkan kelelahan tertentu dari horizon politik radikal.


Menjadikan politik didasarkan pada pengakuan identitas, di satu sisi, dan janji masa depan tentang keselamatan revolusioner, di sisi lain, berarti jatuh ke dalam perangkap kekuasaan negara. Negara difetiskan baik sebagai entitas yang memberikan hak dan status hukum kepada minoritas, maupun sebagai musuh yang harus ditaklukkan agar kebebasan dapat diwujudkan—ilusi yang, sebagaimana ditunjukkan oleh sejarah revolusi, hanya menghasilkan negara-negara baru dan bentuk-bentuk despotisme baru.


Mungkin sudah waktunya untuk meninggalkan “bayangan (spooks)” identitas dan revolusi, serta memikirkan subyektivitas dan politik dengan cara yang berbeda. Di sinilah saya mengusulkan untuk kembali pada filsuf anarkis egois abad ke-19, Max Stirner. Dalam karya

The Ego and Its Own

 (

Der Einzige und sein Eigentum

), yang diterbitkan pada tahun 1844, Stirner mengusulkan bentuk aksi politik alternatif yang ia sebut “Insureksi” (

Insurrection

 atau

Empörung

), yang ia bandingkan dengan Revolusi.


Jika Revolusi adalah proyek yang bertujuan mengubah hubungan sosial dan politik eksternal, maka insureksi adalah transformasi diri. Ini adalah cara bagi individu untuk mengatasi kepatuhan sukarela dan identifikasinya dengan otoritas. Dengan demikian, insureksi tidak menutup kemungkinan terjadinya perubahan sosial dan politik yang lebih luas, tetapi perubahan tersebut didasarkan pada tindakan awal pembebasan diri ini—perubahan dalam cara kita berhubungan dengan diri sendiri dan orang lain.


Sebagaimana dikatakan Stirner, insureksi memiliki konsekuensi tak terhindarkan berupa transformasi keadaan, “namun tidak dimulai dari keadaan tersebut, melainkan dari ketidakpuasan manusia terhadap dirinya sendiri.” Dengan demikian, insureksi dapat dilihat sebagai bentuk emansipasi diri yang radikal. Insureksi tidak dipandu atau ditentukan oleh pelopor revolusioner atau partai-partai, dan ia tidak berusaha merebut serta mengendalikan kekuasaan negara.


Sebaliknya, ia secara radikal anti-institusional: “Revolusi bertujuan pada pengaturan baru; insureksi membawa kita untuk tidak lagi diatur, tetapi mengatur diri kita sendiri, dan tidak menggantungkan harapan pada ‘institusi’.” Negara tidak dilihat sebagai instrumen transformasi sosial, atau bahkan sebagai hambatan utama kebebasan individu. Insureksi menolak fetisisasi kekuasaan negara ini. Individu egois harus menegaskan dirinya di atas negara; ia tidak lagi melihat negara, baik dalam kekaguman maupun ketakutan (dua sisi mata uang yang sama), melainkan hanya pada dirinya sendiri.


Gagasan unik tentang insureksi ini adalah bagian kunci dari proyek filosofis dan etis egoisme Stirner. Bagi Stirner, di dunia yang penuh dengan “bayangan (spooks)” atau abstraksi ideologis dan ideal-ideal metafisik—seperti kemanusiaan, moralitas, kebebasan, hak, masyarakat, hukum, dan negara—yang merupakan sisa-sisa dari agama namun terus menghantui kita, ego adalah satu-satunya realitas konkret, satu-satunya hal yang nyata dan dapat disentuh.


Namun, apa sebenarnya yang dimaksud Stirner dengan ego? Kesalahan umum adalah ketika menyamakannya dengan “individu,” seperti yang sering dilakukan dalam diskursus liberal dan libertarian. Ego jauh lebih cair dan menghindari semua kategorisasi semacam itu atau gagasan “tetap” lainnya. Faktanya, kita dapat mengatakan bahwa ego adalah semacam non-identitas radikal yang tidak dapat dikaitkan dengan bentuk subjektivitas apa pun atau ditentukan oleh karakteristik esensial apa …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Ted Lasso Is Back and Promises To Be Gayer Than Ever
content:
Over three years since the season three finale, Ted Lasso is back! In the fourth season premiere, his old colleagues Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), bisexual baddie Keeley (Juno Temple), and Higgins (Jeremy Swift) come to him with a job offer: coaching their new women’s football team. And as we well know, with women’s soccer comes lesbians, and though we don’t know all the details yet, we know at the very least there will be a lot more queer representation in the coming season than there was in the past few.

What we do know comes mostly from Coach Jackie on TikTok, who was on the red carpet asking the important question to the actors of this season: “Are you playing a lesbian?” Some people were coy about it, but at least two actors already admitted their characters are lesbians, and one actor said she is sadly not playing a lesbian BUT introduced Coach Jackie to her wife, who says she looks like Sue Bird. Also in the cast is nonbinary actor Faye Marsay and Tanya Reynolds, who has played queer before in Sex Education.

Two things people learn quickly upon getting to know me is that men and sports are two of the things I care least about in the world. So it surprised myself as much as anyone else how much I loved the first three seasons of this show. Ted Lasso and his boys kicked their way into my heart one ripped up piece of a BELIEVE sign at a time. I love that it tackled topics like toxic masculinity and homophobia with a lot of honesty and heart. That said, I am REALLY looking forward to a women-dominated season, where I have no doubt they’ll cover topics like sexism and the disparity between men and women’s sports, tucked into its natural charm and humor.

Bonus: It seems the new cast enjoyed their time on set. Tanya Reynolds said, “It’s been a joy to go to work every day, because everyone is so nice.” Adding in my favorite lore drop: “There are no dickheads.”

The first episode of Ted Lasso is available on Apple TV now, with new episodes dropping every Wednesday.

author: Catherine Sostowski Herbes
title: Why Texas v. Kennedy Matters for Disability Rights and Women
content:
Just days after the 36th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), disability rights advocates are warning that one of the nation’s foundational civil rights protections is under threat . The lawsuit Texas v. Kennedy challenges federal regulations implementing Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 , raising concerns about the future of disability rights and independent living.

Passed nearly two decades before the ADA, Section 504 prohibits disability discrimination by programs and institutions that receive federal funding. In 2024, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) updated its regulations to clarify that people with disabilities have the right to receive services in the most integrated setting possible and that governments cannot force people into institutions by failing to provide community-based services.

Nine states, led by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, challenged those regulations in what is now Texas v. Kennedy . These states include Texas, Alaska, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, and South Dakota.

As of July 31, 2026, Missouri, Indiana, South Dakota, and Kansas have formally withdrawn from the complaint, with two rumored to follow. However, the case continues as the remaining plaintiffs seek to overturn the updated rules.

The legal challenge comes as the Trump administration has signaled a broader shift in disability policy. In June, the Department of Justice (DOJ) released a memo questioning the long-standing interpretation of the ADA’s integration mandate established by the Supreme Court in Olmstead v. L.C. (1999).

Although the DOJ’s opinion alone bears no legal authority , disability advocacy groups, such as the Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF) , have raised the alarm , pointing to Texas v. Kennedy and the DOJ memo as potential indications of a department shift away from enforcement of the integration mandate.

These threats against the disabled community are an inherent threat to women everywhere. Women are more likely to be disabled and face long-term health concerns compared to men, due in part to the healthcare industry’s continuous failure to help women, as symptoms are dismissed and medical research centering women is deprioritized. Meanwhile, institutionalization, where a person is committed to a long-term care facility, has a highly gendered past .

As legal challenges to these protections continue, preserving the principles established under Section 504, the ADA, and Olmstead will remain essential to protecting the civil rights and autonomy of millions of Americans.

author: Kelsie kilawna
title: A graduation, a birthday — and an evacuation
content:
My son Skookamina, myself, and my grandmother Barbara P. Marchand. We were celebrating his graduation and her 83rd birthday, two generations marking time together. For her birthday, my grandmother painted portraits of each of us onto canvas bags. She painted us smiling because her prayer for her family has always been that we carry happiness wherever we go. This photo was taken moments before we all had to leave and after most of the family had already left. We didn’t know it then, but we were saying goodbye to ordinary time. Photo by Justin Bambrick


This story is co-published with

The Narwhal

.


Saturday, August 1, started like any other day.


I woke up early with my partner. We sat on the front deck, coffee in hand, watching the morning unfold. We talked about the day ahead, my son Skookamina’s graduation party and my grandmother’s 83rd birthday. There was meat to smoke, cakes to bake, tables to set. The day felt like a blessing because we had so much to celebrate.


I checked my phone. A small fire had started the night before, nothing unusual for this time of year. Our Okanagan Indian Band fire department is amazing. I figured it’d be out by noon, so I kept moving.


I seasoned the meat, I lit the smoker, and I sang while I cooked, the way I always do in my kitchen.


But I kept checking my phone, as we had family that was traveling in for the event.


Mid-morning, we decided as a family to move the party from the beach in town to my uncle’s house in the community. Some of our family had community obligations they’d need to tend to if the fire got out of control. We wanted to be close.


Everyone was there. My grandmother sat in her chair, full of joy as each person arrived. Skookamina was surrounded by his cousins, and the sound of our family filled the air, aunties laughing loud, making outlandish jokes, the familiar banter of people who know each other’s rhythms.


For one hour, we were just a family celebrating,  living our lives the way we always do.


Then, one by one, family members started picking up their phones.


Some stood up. They’d been put on evacuation alert. They had to go home, pack, and wait. I watched them go, first one, then another, then a handful until the room thinned. The laughter quieted and my grandmother sat in her chair, watching her grandchildren leave, one by one. She didn’t say much, she didn’t need to, she knew this dance, she’d done it before.


Eventually, I had to leave too.


We packed the rest of the food. We hugged. We said “see you soon,” and we meant it. Then everyone went home. My father had to evacuate with only minutes to spare. I raced to my dad’s house and we helped him pack what we could as the fire grew at an alarming speed toward him. He was evacuated two minutes from my house, so I knew I was next.


By the time I got home, our family friends were already there, packing for me. They’d already been evacuated without time to take anything with them. Now they were saving us while

their own home

 burned behind them.


One minute I was laughing with my son. The next minute I was grabbing what I could carry. I was not thinking about taking what was valuable, I only grabbed what was irreplaceable. Old ceremony blankets, medicine necklace materials, baskets, photographs, my computers with language recordings, and the eagle feather my son gave me. Everything else I left.


The last photo I took of my house before I left. Four generations, my great great grandmother, my grandfather, my father, me, my son, all held by these walls. I think it’s still standing. I’m grateful for that. But I needed to remember it the way it was, no matter what comes next. Photo by kelsie kilawna


On my way out, I looked back, and the smoke was climbing toward us. Flames moved over the ridge toward my house, and the sky was turning black. I felt an overwhelming need to just get out, this fire had taken on a life of its own.


I could tell this fire doesn’t know our names the way our cultural burns do. It was consuming everything equally, the sacred and the ordinary, the medicine plants and the invasive brush. 


But, even as I watched the fire consume everything in its path, I realized this is exactly what my people prepared me for. This is why they taught me about grief.


They taught me that grief is not a destination, it’s like a creek — you don’t stop it. You discipline yourself to sit beside it, make kin with it, let it flow, and let it carry away what it needs to carry.


They …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: After More Than 20 Years in Prison, Georgia Man Wins New Trial in “Shaken Baby” Case
content:
A Georgia court has

ordered a new trial

 for Danyel Smith, a father who was convicted of killing his two-month-old son, Chandler, more than twenty years ago. Prosecutors relied on a diagnosis of Shaken Baby Syndrome (SBS) to secure his conviction. In recent years, scientific evidence has emerged calling into question the basic assumptions behind the hypothesis.


In her decision, Gwinnett County Superior Court Judge Kimberly A. Gallant ruled that the evolving research into SBS, also known as Abusive Head Trauma (AHT), constitutes new evidence that was not known at the time of trial. 


“Mr. Smith’s evidence is not based on historical facts or eyewitness testimony, but on expert analysis grounded in the application of evolving scientific knowledge,” Gallant wrote in

her decision

. 


Medical experts for the defense

have concluded

 that Chandler was not the victim of abuse.


The defense experts surmise that on the day he fell unconscious, he had a seizure, went into respiratory distress, and stopped breathing. This was at least the second seizure Chandler, who was born five-weeks premature, had experienced, according to Smith’s legal filings. When he was less than two weeks old his mother called 911 and reported that he was breathing strangely and appeared to be having a seizure. The responding paramedics dismissed her concerns. (Smith was not home at the time.)


The expert opinions underlying his motion for a new trial, the judge wrote, “are informed by research advancements in medicine, scientific developments, peer-reviewed literature, and evolving medical standards.”


At the time of Smith’s trial, there was largely a consensus among the scientific and legal communities about the veracity of SBS/AHT. But in the decades since, exonerations and studies have revealed that the so-called

triad of symptoms

 associated with SBS/AHT—bleeding around the eyes, bleeding between the skull and brain, and brain swelling—can be caused by strokes, short-distance falls, childbirth trauma, and disease. 


What was once considered to be virtually unassailable evidence of abuse is now,

in the words of one New Jersey judge

, increasingly understood to be “akin to ‘junk science.’”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


Sign Up


On April 29, 2002, Smith was driving his eight-week-old son, Chandler, to a benefits office so that his partner could apply for food assistance. On the ride over, Smith looked at Chandler when he was stopped at a red light and saw that he was pale and not breathing, according to Smith’s motion for a new trial. Smith’s petition says that in a “frantic phone call” he told his partner that something was wrong with the baby and drove to where she was waiting. 


He carried the baby out of the car and Chandler’s mother called 911. Bystanders attempted to perform CPR. When the paramedics arrived, they took Chandler to the hospital.  


The next day, a child abuse specialist examined Chandler and concluded that he had been shaken. On May 1, Smith was arrested at the hospital. Less than a week later, his son was taken off life support and died.


“[T]here’s no other explanation that the doctors might look for that would explain these symptoms, other than non-accidental trauma, that is, child abuse,” the prosecutor told the jury during opening arguments at Smith’s trial. 


The county medical examiner testified that Chandler’s injuries “are classic and in some cases virtually exclusive for violent shaking.”


Smith maintained his innocence.


“I did not shake my son,” Smith told the jury.


On November 21, 2003, Smith was convicted of felony murder, cruelty to children, and aggravated battery. The judge sentenced him to life in prison.


Smith has never stopped trying to prove his innocence. In 2021, the Southern Center for Human Rights took up his case and began an exhaustive investigation.


In 2021, Smith’s attorneys filed a petition for a new trial, but did not receive an evidentiary hearing until 2024. Prior to the hearing, the Gwinnett County prosecutor’s office

offered Smith a plea deal

. In exchange for pleading guilty, he would get time served and be released from prison, according to Smith’s legal filings. Smith rejected it. 


“He’s now served 24 years in prison, that’s half of his life,” Smith’s attorney, Mark Loudon-Brown, told The Appeal. “During that time, he turned down the opportunity to go home simply …

author: Admin101
title: The Platform at 100: Voices of Organized Anarchists Around the Globe (Vol. 2)
content:
To mark the 100 year anniversary of the publication of the

Platform of Libertarian Communists (Draft)

, we are excited to present the second in a three volume series of interviews discussing the document’s lasting legacy with anarchist organizations around the world

.


The Platform, as it is often called by shorthand, was written by a group of Russian and Ukranian anarchists exiled in the wake of the Bolshevik seizure of state power during the 1917 October Revolution. The document was meant to be a corrective to the prevailing anarchist orthodoxy of the time, which its authors—including

Nestor Makhno

 and other active participants in the revolution—believed had led to their defeat.


Note:

 Originally we had planned to release all of the interviews in two volumes. However, the number of organizations who requested to participate


and the length of the content requires us to break the interviews up into three volumes.


The

first volume

 covered organizations in the Americas,

this second volume covers organizations in Europe

, and the third will cover organizations in Asia and Oceania.


This project is a collaboration between the External Education and International Relations Committees of Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN).


Table of Contents

Introduction

Union Communiste Libertaire (France)

Die Plattform (Germany)

Anarchist Communist Group (UK)

Midada (Switzerland)

Liza (Spain)

Embat (Catalonia)


Download


the Pamphlet

Version


Introduction


2026 marks 100 years since the publication of the

Organizational Platform of the Libertarian Communists (Draft)

 by the Dielo Truda (Workers’ Cause) group. The document, written by Russian, Belarusian, and Ukrainian anarchists exiled in the wake of the 1917 October Revolution in Russia, is known for the sharp revisions it applied to the contemporary anarchist orthodoxy. Though criticized by some of the most prominent anarchist thinkers of the period,

the Platform

 (as it has come to be known by shorthand) represents a first serious attempt to grapple with organizational and strategic shortcomings in the anarchist movement, exposed by its direct involvement in a large-scale revolutionary upheaval.


While it is true that the Dielo Truda group set a course distinct from many of their anarchist contemporaries, the novelty of the principles put forward in the Platform is often overstated. The central concern of the Platform’s authors was a more effective coordination of anarchist militants aiming to intervene in social movements. The Dielo Truda group arrived at the conclusion that this could only be achieved through the construction of a revolutionary political organization. Indeed, this same insight was achieved by Mikhail Bakunin more than half a century earlier as he helped to found the Alliance of Socialist Democracy, which was later dissolved into the International Workingmen’s Association (also known as the First International). In other words, far from being a recent invention, the anarchist embrace of formal revolutionary political organization can be traced back to the movement’s origins.


Today we recognize this insight as ‘organizational dualism,’ a phrase that refers to the necessity of, and reciprocal relationship between, revolutionary political organization and mass organization. While organizations interviewed in this survey may identify to a greater or lesser extent with a particular historical framework—most commonly platformism or especifismo—all hold the organizational dualist principle as a central tenet.


Union Communiste Libertaire

 (France)


1.


UCL was formed in 2019 as a fusion of two existing organizations,

Coordination des Groupes Anarchistes (CGA)

 and Alternative Libertaire (AL). Can you briefly explain what brought these two groups together and what the process of becoming one organization involved?


UCL:

AL and CGA were two relatively small organisations. They didn’t have the exact same background but they shared theoretical references and a similar intervention into the global struggle of the people. 


The growth of both organizations was slowing. Both organizations got used to working together, and the election of Emmanuel Macron meant a strengthening of attacks against the working class. For our political tradition, the organization isn’t the be-all and end-all of our political activity but a tool in the service of our movement. It felt natural to attempt a fusion.

content: ﻿ Born out of the Korean diaspora in Manchuria escaping brutal Japanese colonial rule and in the power vacuum left in the wake of the assassination of the local warlord, the Korean Anarchist Federation existed against all odds.
