author: AWSM
title: A Community in the Cracks of Capitalism
content:
A piece of Christchurch that the property market abandoned after the earthquakes has become home to people abandoned by the property market. The old Bexley neighbourhood was largely cleared after liquefaction made conventional residential development impossible. Houses disappeared, streets remained and the land sat waiting for whatever official purpose would eventually be found for it. Into that gap came people who needed somewhere to live. They arrived in cars, vans, buses and tents. Some were working. Some were retired. Some had children. They did what people have always done when the institutions around them fail, they improvised. A community grew. Earlier this year about 40 people were living around Wetlands Grove; reports now put the number at more than 100. Christchurch City Council has told them they must leave by 28 February 2027 because the area is intended for wetland development. There is an obvious temptation to treat this as a story about homelessness, council planning or the difficulties of finding somewhere suitable for a group of people living in vehicles. It is all of those things, but underneath them sits a much simpler question. What is land for? The answer given by our economic system is that land belongs to whoever has legal title to it, and its legitimate use is determined by owners, planners and institutions. The people actually living on it remain secondary. They may sleep there, look after one another there and make the place usable through their own effort, but none of that gives them any meaningful claim to it. Their relationship to the place exists only for as long as the legal owner tolerates it. That distinction between ownership and use lies close to the heart of the anarchist criticism of private property.

The people living at Wetlands Grove have already demonstrated something that governments spend enormous amounts of money trying unsuccessfully to manufacture through policy documents – people can organise social life themselves. Earlier reporting described an informal community growing around buses, vans and cars, with neighbours helping one another through winter and a communal tent being established as shared space. One man who had been sleeping in a small tent was helped into an old car when the cold became severe. Council rubbish collection and portable toilets made conditions more bearable, but the social organisation of the place came largely from the people living there. Moko, one of the informal figures in the community, was working full-time on an on-call road crew. Others were pensioners. Ngawai Timu described abandoning a $470-a-week rental because she felt she was spending her life paying somebody else’s mortgage. Polly Stewart was surviving on the pension in a bus. Families were living there too, including a woman with several children living from a bus. These details matter because homelessness is constantly spoken about as though it were primarily a pathology of homeless people. Addiction, mental illness, poor budgeting, antisocial behaviour and bad choices are summoned as explanations because those explanations leave the social order intact. They allow us to imagine that housed people possess some quality that homeless people lack. Wetlands Grove makes that story harder to sustain. When people with jobs cannot obtain housing, when pensioners decide rent leaves too little for ordinary life, and when families find themselves competing with dozens of others for a private rental, the problem is no longer plausibly located inside the individual. There are certainly people living rough who struggle with addiction or serious psychological distress. There are also people who get up and go to work from a tent. A housing system that cannot reliably house either has failed at the most elementary level.

New Zealand has become remarkably skilled at describing this failure without challenging the institution producing it. We talk about housing supply, affordability pressures and housing need. We devise eligibility categories and waiting lists. We construct administrative pathways through emergency housing, transitional housing, community housing and social housing. Every stage acquires its own assessments and rules. The language becomes more sophisticated while people remain without homes. At the 2023 Census, Statistics New Zealand estimated that at least 112,496 people were experiencing severe housing deprivation, around 2.3 percent of the usually resident population. The …

author: Yasmine Johnson
title: Royal Commission puts pro-Palestine protesters on trial
content:
The Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion held a one-day hearing block on protests and policing on 4 August. Like the rest of the commission, it was more a prosecution than an inquiry: the Palestine solidarity movement was on trial, and its opponents were invited to act as judge, jury and witness. 

The commission has already been filled with unsubstantiated and unchallenged testimony from so-called lived experience witnesses, often from pro-Israel lobby organisations. It is a platform for those wishing to slander the Palestine movement as antisemitic. In this hearing block, the fix was in from the beginning. Despite nearly three years of protests involving many thousands of people, the commission declared that just two protests would be discussed: a Sydney protest on 9 October 2023 that marched to the Opera House and a Nazi rally held by the National Socialist Network outside NSW Parliament on 8 November 2025. 

The latter barely warranted a mention in the commission. It was fitting, given that one of the key, and outrageous, arguments pursued by pro-Israel organisations is that the left, rather than the far right, are the antisemites. This is in keeping with Israel’s alignment to extreme right-wing governments and parties around the world. Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism Jillian Segal, whose family has bankrolled far-right organisation Advance Australia, failed to put out a single statement of condemnation of the Nazi rally. The Nazis weren’t the subject of the hearing: they were props in an argument about the left. The point of including this rally was not to confront the far right, but to attempt to tarnish the Palestine movement by association. 

The main purpose of this block was to re-air the lies told about the 9 October Opera House protest, and to rake the police over the coals for “transferring control of the CBD to protesters”. The main two witnesses called were not people who had actually witnessed anything that night. One was David Ossip, president of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, a pro-Israel organisation. The other was the assistant commissioner of NSW Police, Peter McKenna. Not a single protester or protest organiser was invited to give evidence. Despite all this, proceedings did not go exactly as planned.

Ossip argued that the protest was “appalling” because it took place while Israeli civilians were being killed following the Hamas attack on 7 October. He apparently couldn’t understand why anyone might want to protest, given that Israel had not even begun any military operations by that time. This claim has been made several times at the commission, supposedly showing that people were not really protesting against occupation and a coming genocide, but celebrating the gruesome deaths of Israelis. The problem is that it is not true, and this was pointed out to Ossip in cross-examination by lawyers for the Palestine Action Group (PAG) and the Australian Palestine Advocacy Network (APAN). 

Prior to the attack in October, 2023 was already the deadliest year for Palestinians living in the West Bank since records began, with more than 200 killed in racist pogroms by extremist settlers and Israeli soldiers. For this reason, PAG had already organised five demonstrations by this point in 2023. 

By the evening of 7 October, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had already declared war, promising “mighty vengeance for this black day ... We will target all of Hamas's positions. We will turn Gaza into a deserted island. To the citizens of Gaza, I say. You must leave now. We will target each and every corner of the strip”. Two hundred and thirty Palestinians were killed by Israeli airstrikes on Gaza on that day alone. By 9 October, more than 400 had been killed in Gaza, a total blockade of food, water, fuel and medical supplies had been imposed, and Israel was openly preparing a ground invasion. Incredibly, when confronted with these facts, Ossip doubled down on his false claim that Israel had not commenced military operations.

The right has responded to Ossip's evidence with outrage. Not outrage that he would double down on false claims, under oath, in order to demonise a mass movement against genocide, but outrage that he could be challenged on his false claims at all. author: Sheree Lowe
title: Our Children are the Treaty generation
content:
This

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day

, we have an opportunity to reflect on something remarkable. 


Across Victoria, our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are growing up in one of the most significant political moments since colonisation. They are the first generation of children to grow up in

Victoria’s Treaty era

. Treaty is about far more than legal agreements or institutional reform. At its heart, Treaty is about people, and most importantly, our children, and our future generations. 


The true measure of any Treaty will not be found in the number of agreements reached or milestones achieved. It will be measured by whether it truly improves the lives of future generations. 


Will Aboriginal children grow up healthier? Will their identity and Connection to their Culture be strong? Will they have every opportunity to learn, thrive and lead? Will they inherit systems that recognise their strengths rather than focus on their disadvantage? 


These are the questions that really matter. 


Aboriginal children already possess extraordinary strengths. They inherit the oldest continuing culture on Earth. They are surrounded by families, Elders and Communities who pass on knowledge, stories and traditions – keeping them strong and keeping them connected to who they are. 


But despite their strengths, many Aboriginal children continue to experience inequitable outcomes across

health

, education,

incarceration

, and wellbeing. Too often, systems have been designed to exclude Aboriginal people and their families, rather than include them.  


Treaty is our chance to change this.  


Treaty allows us to shift decision-making closer to Aboriginal communities, strengthening self-determination and creating services that better reflect the aspirations, cultures and needs of Aboriginal children and families. 


This is not simply about changing policies. It is about changing possibilities. 


Imagine growing up as an Aboriginal child.

Imagine instead of growing up in a State that perpetuates stigma, stereotypes and wants to dismiss your culture in dark history books – you grow up knowing who you are, where you belong and actually understanding your Country and Culture.  


Children have the potential to grow up in a state where their Culture is not only respected but embedded throughout education, healthcare and public life.  Our collective history recognised, our languages celebrated and Community empowered to shape the services that support our families. 


Imagine knowing that decisions about your future are increasingly made by your own people, your Community.

That is the promise that Treaty represents. 


For today’s Aboriginal children, this is not some distant vision. It is unfolding right now, during their own childhood. 


They are the first generation who will remember Victoria before Treaty, and who will one day tell their own children what it was like to witness this historic transformation. 


That is both exciting and humbling, but it also places an extraordinary responsibility on all of us. 


Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day reminds us that children are not just our future leaders – they are citizens of today. Their experiences matter. Their ideas matter. Their voices matter. 


If Treaty is truly about creating a better future, then Aboriginal children must remain at the centre of every conversation. 


Because when today’s children become tomorrow’s Elders, they will not judge this generation by the complexity of negotiations or the wording of agreements. 


They will judge us by outcomes. 


Did we create a Victoria where Aboriginal children could grow up proud of who they are? Did we ensure they remained connected to Culture, Country and Community?  Did we reduce the inequities they inherited? Did we create opportunities for every Aboriginal child and their family to flourish and thrive? 


The answers to those questions will be the enduring measure of success. 


So, this Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day, let us recognise that our children are growing up during a defining chapter in our state’s history, and work together to ensure it’s done right.


We all must take pride in being the first Australian state to take this historic step and ensure that Treaty is not repealed after the state election. 


Because Treaty is a promise to our future generations.  


A promise that they are not simply growing up in the era of Treaty …

author: James Plested
title: ‘Ready to fight for a socialist future’: eight hundred attend Victorian Socialists’ campaign launch
content:
It was the biggest event the Victorian Socialists (VS) have put on since we formed in 2018. On Saturday, 1 August, 800 people turned out to the Aborigines Advancement League in the northern Melbourne suburb of Thornbury to help us launch our campaign for the 2026 state election. Tickets were selling so fast in the week leading up to it that we had to scramble to ensure the bigger-than-expected crowd could be properly accommodated.

It’s a long time since the socialist movement in Australia has had to deal with an issue like this, and it was hard not to feel, on the night, that something significant has changed. The evening’s compere, VS candidate for Northcote Kath Larkin, expressed the feeling in her opening remarks. “We know that this election will not be easily won”, she said, “but if tonight is anything to go by, we’ve got masses of people who are ready to fight for a socialist future”.

For decades now the numbers of people concluding that the major problems in society are caused by capitalism, and that it’s socialist politics and organising that provide the answers, have never really gone beyond a slow drip. But watching the movement of hundreds of people up and down the steps leading into the central part of the launch venue evoked—in this hopeful mind at least—something like a waterfall. I’d have settled for a steady stream, but this felt like something more than that.

Despite the multiplying and deepening crises of capitalism afflicting society today, we know the fortunes of our movement won’t change just overnight. “The tradition of all dead generations weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living”, as Marx put it in

The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte

. Part of that nightmare, for us, is the widespread sense of hopelessness and passivity in the face of the many obvious problems of society—a product of decades of one-sided class war being waged by the capitalist class and their political servants against working-class people, the poor and the oppressed.

There’s no shortage of people who feel, on some level, that something is very wrong with society. The problem is, very few think there’s anything much we can do about it. So, a big part of what we were trying to do at the launch was rekindle a sense of hope for the future and a belief that if working-class people stand up, get organised and fight back, then we can achieve the kind of radical change our society so desperately needs.

This was a dominant theme of all the speeches. Public school teacher and VS candidate for Niddrie Brendan Laws, who is running against the former Labor education minister and now Premier Ben Carroll, talked about it in connection with his work as a leader of the Socialists in Schools rank-and-file union group. “We organised Socialists in Schools”, he said, “to be the dogged fighters, to raise expectations, to assuage the fears about striking, [and] to let people know what power we have ... This year we’ve had this huge segment of workers get a bit more confidence, and it is now the most urgent task to translate that into the fight for the whole new society that we deserve”.

VS candidate for Footscray Jasmine Duff, who as a convener of Students for Palestine has played a central role in the Palestine solidarity movement, spoke similarly. “Socialism is about saying we deserve better”, she said. “We deserve a world of dignity, and we deserve a world where our lives aren’t measured by what we produce for the capitalists.”

The path to re-establishing socialism as a genuine fighting force in Australian political life is a long one. It will require the collective intellect and energy of thousands of committed socialist activists devoting themselves to our cause, not just for this election campaign, but for years and decades into the future. 

As we move along that path, however, it’s important to mark the moments that feel like genuine milestones. The VS launch was one such moment—providing exactly the spark of inspiration needed as we embark on what we hope will be a historic, breakthrough campaign.

James Plested is the Victorian Socialists communications director.

author: Susan Price
title: Peru: Far-right Fujimori sworn in as president, amid protests
content:
Keiko Fujimori, leader of the far-right Popular Force party, was sworn in as Peru’s president on July 28, after narrowly defeating leftist candidate Roberto Sánchez in the run-off election in June.

Fujimori is the daughter of former dictator Alberto Fujimori, who imposed a United States-sponsored “shock therapy” in the 1990s, privatising public enterprises, eliminating state subsidies, further deregulating the economy and attacking labour laws.

Fujimori represents the continuation of her father’s policies and has maintained the neoliberal status quo through her party’s control of Congress since 2016 and other state institutions, such as the judiciary.

In her first address, Fujimori pledged to combat “insecurity” and has previously promised to fight crime with an “iron fist”. She said the military will take control during “states of emergency”, which have been used by successive right-wing governments to suspend freedom of assembly, movement and privacy.

The falsity of Fujimori’s supposed “anti-crime” agenda is laid bare by her and her party’s record of brazen corruption and facilitating organised crime. She was imprisoned in pre-trial detention for her role in the Odebrecht bribery scandal and for using illicit money to fund presidential campaigns. As president, she is now immune from prosecution.

Moreover, 15 of Fujimori’s 19 cabinet members have faced criminal investigations or been imprisoned for corruption, theft, fraud, embezzlement and assault. Vice President Luis Galarreta is currently under investigation for money laundering, abuse of authority and links to organised crime, while environment minister Vladimiro Huaroc has 51 investigations against him.

Fujimori’s supposed “tough-on-crime” approach also does not extend to the heinous crimes committed by the police and military when inflicting violence against Peru’s working class.

The Fujimorista-controlled Congress approved Law 32735 on July 21, which allows crimes committed by the police and military to be investigated and tried by police and military courts. Ongoing investigations and trials can now be transferred from civilian courts or stopped, including cases where police and military have already been convicted.

This adds to the widespread impunity already enjoyed by police and soldiers, who have killed at least 50 people in anti-government protests since 2022. Recently, a police officer shot and killed an eight-year-old boy in Huacho, a town about 150 kilometres north of Lima.

During her address, Fujimori lamented that Peru’s economic inequality is the highest in Latin America and pledged, in a populist move, to raise the minimum wage by 15%, to 1300 soles (A$545) a month. She knows this will have a negligible impact on big business bottom lines and workers’ living standards, in a country where more than 70% work in the informal economy, with no guaranteed minimum wage and basic work entitlements.

In many ways, Fujimori and her father are responsible for entrenching the neoliberal model that makes Peru one of the most unequal countries in the world. The top 1% control almost half (44.7%) of the country’s wealth, while the bottom 50% control just 0.1%.

Under this model, domestic and transnational corporations are granted almost free reign to pillage the country’s vast mineral deposits to make obscene profits.

Meanwhile, the concentration of the economy into monopolies and oligopolies — particularly in the agribusiness industry — results in price fixing and rising living costs. The basic family basket — the cost of basic goods and services for a family of four for a month — is more than 1860 soles ($779.29), which Fujimori’s promised wage raise covers less than 70% of.

Joining the far-right shift in governments in the region, Fujimori seeks to deepen ties with the United States and other far-right leaders in the region. Her inauguration was attended by far-right leaders, such as Chilean President José Antonio Kast and Argentine President Javier Milei.

She pledged to join US President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas, which aims to reassert US economic and military dominance in Latin America.

Thousands protested in the country’s capital, Lima, against Fujimori’s inauguration, rightly pointing out her role in introducing laws that facilitate crime and grant impunity to the military and police. Among the protesters were relatives of some of the thousands of people tortured, killed and disappeared under her father’s regime.

During …

title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #294 w Émile P. Torres on TESCREAL & the techno-fascist redux : July 23, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Dr. Émile P. Torres [Bluesky]. Émile is an author (most recently of the book Human Extinction: A History of the Science and Ethics of Annihilation), podcaster (Dystopia Now) and critic of the bundle of ideologies collectively known as TESCREAL: Transhumanism, Extropianism, Singularitarianism, Cosmism, Rationalism, Effective Altruism and Longtermism.

We first spoke to Émile about TESCREAL in October 2023. A few years later, we reviewed the situation in 2026 and discussed the rollout of AI (‘It must nestle everywhere, settle everywhere, establish connexions everywhere’!), AGI, ASI and the speculative fictions of Silicon Valley.

title: Iran launches missile strike on Komala headquarters in South Kurdistan
content:
Ehmed Hisên Pena, a Central Committee member of the Kurdistan Toilers’ Community (Komala), stated that Iran has once again launched a missile attack on the headquarters of Komala in the Geliyê Alaneyê area at around 1:30 p.m.


Pena added, “So far, there is no official information on whether the attack caused any fatalities or injuries.”


Stating that Iran’s attacks were ongoing, Pena said the strike was part of a broader campaign of missile and drone attacks targeting the bases of East Kurdistan (Rojhilat) parties located in Bashur.


According to the organization’s records, the total number of missiles and drones directed against Komala camps since the outbreak of the war between Iran and the United States has exceeded 102, Pena added.

author: CNT Galiza
title: Paco Ponzán: anarcosindicalismo, revolución y resistencia
content:
La vida de Francisco Ponzán Vidal (Oviedo, 30/03/1911 – Buzet-sur-Tarn, Francia, 17/08/1944) revela el compromiso constante del movimiento anarquista ibérico con la transformación de la sociedad, antes y después del golpe de Estado franquista, así como con la lucha antifascista, que aún hoy conserva gran relevancia. Maestro de profesión, militante de la CNT y destacado organizador anarquista, Ponzán centró su vida en la revolución social y la solidaridad internacional, tanto durante la Guerra Civil como posteriormente en la Resistencia francesa contra el nazismo.


Aunque nació en Oviedo, su familia pronto se trasladó a Huesca. Allí creció y, años más tarde, influenciado por la biblioteca de su padre y las conversaciones con un profesor, conoció a Ramón Acín, figura histórica de la CNT en Huesca, quien lo introdujo en el pensamiento anarquista. Esta intensa amistad perduró hasta 1936, año en que Acín y su compañera, la también anarquista Concha Monrás, fueron torturados y fusilados por los fascistas.


Desde muy joven, Ponzán participó en el Ateneo Cultural Libertario de la ciudad. Estudió magisterio, título que obtuvo con apenas dieciocho años. Su primer trabajo como maestro lo llevó al pueblo de Ipas, cerca de Jaca, donde vivió de cerca el clima político de la Segunda República en la región. En diciembre de 1930, se produjo el levantamiento republicano contra la monarquía corrupta, conocido como el Levantamiento de Jaca, liderado por los capitanes Fermín Galán y Ángel García Hernández, que marcó el inicio de una fuerte escalada represiva contra los militantes revolucionarios. A partir de entonces, las detenciones de Ponzán por la policía y la guardia civil se hicieron cada vez más frecuentes debido a su participación en huelgas y movilizaciones obreras.


Enviado a Mazaricos en 1934, al principio la distancia le dificultó el contacto con sus camaradas de la CNT de La Coruña; pero el problema se resolvió en febrero de 1936 con su traslado a Camelle, donde se unió al grupo de Noia. Las notas del sacerdote de Ponte do Porto, quien seguramente lo envidiaba, datan de este período, pues anota sobre Ponzán: «

Hace exactamente un año que organizó, con el conocimiento y la paciencia de las autoridades, una procesión religiosa precedida por él, en burla del día del Espíritu Santo en Camelle

». Estas palabras se añadieron poco después a otras notas en su expediente de purga, donde se le acusa de ser una «

persona muy peligrosa» que «estuvo a punto de llevarnos hacia un sovietismo libertario local

» e incluso de ser «

más amigo de los explosivos que de los libros de texto para la enseñanza

». Entre el delirio y la crueldad de estas notas, se puede reconocer, al menos, que demuestran no solo el grado de cobardía de quienes, poco después, iban a asolar el país, sino también la capacidad organizativa de una clase obrera con una conciencia cada vez más crítica.


El golpe militar de julio de 1936 lo sorprendió en Huesca, donde había ido a pasar sus vacaciones tras adelantarlas, pues ya percibía un ambiente general preocupante. La ciudad fue tomada inmediatamente por los golpistas, por lo que tuvo que huir a territorio republicano.


Allí, Ponzán asumió responsabilidades políticas dentro de las instituciones creadas por el movimiento anarquista en Aragón, en una experiencia singular de autogobierno promovida por la CNT, basada en la colectivización de la economía, la democracia directa y la organización popular. Fue primero Ministro de Transportes y Comunicaciones en el Consejo Regional de Defensa y posteriormente se incorporó a la Subsecretaría de Información y Propaganda del Consejo de Aragón, dirigida por el también anarquista Evaristo Viñuales.


Con el avance de la guerra, la tensión entre las organizaciones revolucionarias y los sectores partidarios de la centralización del poder se intensificó progresivamente. El PCE, fortalecido por la ayuda soviética, optó por militarizar las milicias y subordinar la revolución a los objetivos militares de la República. Por el contrario, la CNT y el POUM defendieron una revolución social inseparable de la lucha contra el fascismo.


El enfrentamiento alcanzó su punto álgido en los sucesos de mayo de 1937 en Barcelona. Ponzán participó en la defensa de las posiciones anarquistas durante los combates callejeros hasta que fue arrestado por las fuerzas comunistas. Incluso fue llevado al pelotón de fusilamiento, del que logró escapar gracias a otros militantes anarquistas. El posterior …

author: Daron Letts
title: Unionized QEC workers get 18% increase over 4 years
content:
The Nunavut Employees Union and Qulliq Energy Corp., the territory’s electricity supplier, have ratified a new four-year collective agreement, which

 includes a wage increase of 18 per cent over four years, increased continuous service bonuses and expanded leave provisions.


“The new collective agreement shows what’s possible when we work together to improve workplaces and working conditions for employees who keep the lights on in Nunavut communities.” said Jason Rochon, Nunavut Employees Union president, in a news release issued Monday.


The agreement, ratified Aug. 6, includes a wage increase of 12 per cent, effective Jan. 1, 2025. Annual increases of two per cent follow in 2026, 2027 and 2028.


A provision in the contract that allows for Inuit cultural pursuit leave, which gives Inuit workers paid time off to engage in hunting, fishing, harvesting and other traditional activities, increased to three days from two.


“This agreement provides stability that will benefit our employees

and our communities in the years ahead,” wrote Gwen Healey Akearok, minister responsible for the Qulliq Energy Corp., in the release.


Negotiations for a new contact began in September 2025. A tentative agreement was achieved in May, and t

he union held ratification meetings in late June in Cambridge Bay, Iqaluit, Rankin Inlet, Baker Lake and online.

author: Ahmed Ashmawy
title: Alexandria’s Amreya shuts factory to striking workers
content:
Workers sought intervention from authorities on Sunday after management at Misr al-Amreya Spinning and Weaving Company in Alexandria decided to suspend operations at the factory indefinitely, according to four workers who spoke to Mada Masr.


The management’s statement said the shutdown was to allow for routine maintenance, inventory and reviews. But the workers said they view the move as punishment for their ongoing strike against under-payment.


How did the strike begin? 


Hundreds of workers at the company, which is

owned

 by Banque Misr,

began

 a strike in late July, to protest the miscalculation of a “special allowance” bonus to which they are entitled.


The workers told Mada Masr at the time that the company is calculating their bonuses as a percentage of their baseline wages, rather than as a percentage of their insured wages — effectively reducing the bonus value. 


The base wage is around a third of the value of the insured wage, as per a worker’s payslip that Mada Masr reviewed last month.


A new social insurance

law

 ratified in July obliges public sector companies to pay a “special allowance” bonus and to calculate it at the rate of 12 percent of the insured wage. Worker representatives speaking to Mada Masr last week

said

 that the company owner has said Amreya is a private company exempt from the requirement, but the head of the company’s workers union committee, Mohamed al-Sawy, told Mada Masr that the company committed to an agreement five years ago that it would keep worker privileges at Amreya consistent with those in the public sector.


Throughout the strike, management and the company’s union committee

tried

 to persuade workers to return to their jobs while their demands were being considered. The workers refused, and some received implicit threats, their representatives told Mada Masr. One quoted his manager as telling him, “What’s coming is not going to be good.”


Management issued a notice on Thursday saying it was “continuously examining and studying the legitimate rights of workers” in order to present their findings to the relevant authorities. The notice added that these rights “are safeguarded through unity.”


The striking workers rejected what came in the notice, as it did not specify any clear action or timeline for implementing their demands, according to the workers.


Management shuts company premises to workers


It was the following day that the Alexandria company’s management issued a notice suspending work, restricting attendance to “workers who are called in to manage the extensive inventorying operations,” while “salaries and wages stipulated by law will continue to be paid on their scheduled dates.”


Copy of Misr al-Amreya Spinning and Weaving Company management’s Friday notice.


On Saturday morning, employees tried to reach work by public transportation after the company withheld the buses that normally transport them to work from different areas, according to the workers. But police, deployed heavily at the railway crossing leading to the gate, blocked them from reaching the factory.


Fearing wage deductions over the closure, some workers went to the police station to file incident reports and lodged complaints with the labor office over their demands and the closure decision. Others filed similar complaints on Sunday.


The four company workers who spoke to Mada Masr said they were among those filing complaints with their local labor directorate on Sunday over management’s indefinite suspension of operations at the factory.


Amreya previously

closed

 its factory for a month in 2015 after workers went on strike to demand the payment of incentives and bonuses in line with those granted at other companies in the spinning and weaving sector.


Workers at Amreya also

staged

a strike in February over wage reductions, which took the form of higher taxes and increased social insurance

deductions

. In April, they

went

on strike again, demanding higher wages, an increase in production bonuses and higher hazard pay.

Alexandria’s Amreya shuts factory to striking workers

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

author: Unknown
title: ABD: "Sosyalistler halka kulak verdikleri için kazanıyor"
content:
2026 ara seçimlerine bir kaç ay kala, ABD siyasetinde bir sosyalist heyula kol geziyor. İki partili Trump ve MAGA Cumhuriyetçilerin popülist sağcılığı karşısında bir dönem bocalayan Demokrat Parti'nin 2024 yenilgisi sonrasında muhalefette yeniden başını kaldırmasında sosyalistlerin rolü giderek belirginleşiyor. New York Belediye Başkanlığını Trump'ın desteklediği Demokrat Partili rakibini yenilgiye uğratarak kazanan Mamdani'nin zaferinden sonra sosyalistlerin başını çektiği, tabanın söz ve kararına dayalı çalışma tarzı gitgide partinin yönünü daha derinden belirlemeye başlıyor. 


Toplumsal sorunlar üzerine çarpıcı denemeleriyle tanınan New York Times köşe yazarı, sosyolog ve kültür eleştirmeni Profesör Tressie McMillan Cottom, bu süreci çevirisini sunduğumuz "Sosyalistler halka kulak verdikleri için kazanıyor" başlıklı makalesiyle değerlendiriyor.


Amerikan siyasetinde sosyalist bir canlanmaya mı tanık oluyoruz?


Zohran Mamdani'nin New York Belediye Başkanı seçilmesinden bu yana yapılan siyasi tahlilleri toparladığınızda solculuğun altın çağında yaşadığınıza ya da komünistlerin gelmekte olduğuna inanasınız gelebilir.


Solcu adayların önseçim başarıları


Bu tablo, gün gelip seçim sonuçlarına da yansıyabilir; ama o gün bugün değil. Evet, bu hafta pek çok solcu aday başarılı oldu; Michigan ve Kansas'ta dikkat çekici ön seçim zaferleri kazanıldı, ama yarışı kazananların arasında pek çok ılımlı Demokrat da vardı. Kazanan adaylardan bazılarının kampanya bütçesi oldukça yüksekti. Diğerleri ise son derece büyük bir mali sıkıntıyla başa çıkmak zorundaydı. Ancak içlerindeki en iyiler, Demokratların kazanmak için yalnızca seçmenlerden bağış toplamakla kalmayıp onları örgütlemeleri gerektiğinin idrakinde kampanya yürütenlerdi.


Demokrat Partinin yapısal sorunları


Demokrat Parti derin bir yapısal sorunla karşı karşıya. Bir yanda özlemini duyduğu geçmiş, öte yanda ise henüz kuramadığı bir gelecek var. Şimdilik bunun farkında olan yalnızca partinin ilerici kanadı gibi görünüyor.


Düzen içi Demokrat Partililer, solcu adayların seçilebilirliği konusunda istedikleri kadar gürültü koparsalar da, partinin halletmesi gereken daha büyük meseleleri var. Demokratların seçim gücünün iki kaynağından biri olan işçi hareketi, New Deal'den sonraki on yıllar boyunca işçi sınıfından erkeklerin oylarını güvence altına almış ve kırsal bölgelerde, ABD'nin kuzeydoğusu ile Büyük Göller çevresinde yer alan, 20. Yüzyılın büyük bölümünde ülkenin ağır sanayi merkezi olan, ancak 1970'lerden itibaren hızlı sanayisizleşme yaşayan bölgelere verilen adla Rust Belt'te (Pas Kuşağı) Demokratların ana damarı olarak iş görmüştü. Sivil haklar örgütleri ise, Kennedy’nin öldürülmesinden sonra başa geçen Demokrat Başkan Lyndon B. Johnson’ın Sivil Haklar Yasası'nı imzaladığı günden beri bekleceği şekilde Siyahların oylarını güvence altına alarak Demokratların Güney'de rekabeti sürdürebilmesini sağlamıştı. Uzun yıllar boyunca sıradan Demokrat adaylar, karmaşık siyasal mesajlarını seçmene ulaştırma işini büyük ölçüde bu iki örgütlü toplumsal güce bıraktı.


Demokrat Parti'nin kendi sınırlarına varması


Anlaşılması gereken en önemli şey, peş peşe  60 yıl boyunca biriken ekonomik, hukuksal, siyasal ve kültürel zorlukların sendikalar ve sivil hak gruplarının bu görevi yerine getirmesini artık imkânsız değilse de çok güç kılmış olması.


Özellikle siyah sivil haklar örgütleri uzun zamandır Demokrat Parti'nin örgütlenmesi  için büyük çaba gösteriyor. Sadece sandığa gitmekle kalmıyor, seçmen yetiştiriyor, ulusal platformları yerel mesajlarla dönüştürüyor ve adaylarla çalışanları eğitiyor. Demokrat Parti'nin seçim makinesini ayakta tutanlar, kiliselerde ışıkları söndürmeyenler, minibüsleri kullanan, mahalle mahalle dolaşan, mitinglere katılan ve seçim günü seçmeni güvenle sandığa taşıyanlar siyah kadınlardı. Güney'deki siyah örgütçüler, Yüksek Mahkeme tarafından Oy Hakkı Yasası’nın budanmasından sonra Demokratların bir süvari kıtası gibi yardıma koşmasını bekliyordu. Oysa şimdi kendilerini terk edilmiş hissediyorlar. Muhafazakârların savunuculuk ve lobi örgütü Heritage Action ile kampüslerde ve seçim kampanyalarında faaliyet gösteren gençlik ve siyasi aktivizm örgütü Turning Point USA gibi gruplara bakıp, bakıp, "Bizim de böyle kurumlarımız olsaydı" diye hayıflanıyorlar.


Sendikalı işçilerin oranı da rekor düzeyde düşük. Demokratlar işçi sınıfı seçmenlerini geri kazanacak ve Güney'i harekete geçirecek, seçim kazandıracak merkezci bir mesaj bulsalar bile, seçmeni …

author: Unknown
title: Almanya’da ırkçı AfD partisi bir eyalette iktidara yürüyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Oxfordian Kissuth/Wikimedia

Önümüzdeki eylül ayında Almanya’nın dört eyaletinde sandık kurulacak. 6 Eylül’de doğu eyaleti Saksonya-Anhalt, 13 Eylül’de Aşağı Saksonya eyaletleri sandık başına gidecek. 20 Eylül’de ise başkent ve aynı zamanda eyalet olan Berlin’de ve ülkenin kuzeydoğu eyaleti Mecklenburg-Vorpommern’de seçimler gerçekleştirilecek.

Saksonya-Anhalt seçimlerinde ırkçı parti AfD’nin önde olması ve ilk defa bir eyalette yönetime gelmesi ihtimali ise tartışma yarattı. DW Türkçe’nin haberine göre anketler AfD’nin oyunun yüzde 42’ye kadar yükseldiğine işaret ediyor.

Bu eyalette “kesinleşmiş aşırı sağ aşırılıkçı grup” olarak sınıflandırılan parti, Almanya genelinde de “aşırı sağ aşırılıkçılık” şüphesiyle istihbarat örgütü olan Anayasayı Koruma Teşkilatı’nın gözetimi altında. Partinin gençlik oluşumu ise federal düzeyde “aşırı sağ” olarak sınıflandırılmıştı.

Saksonya-Anhalt’ta AfD’nin sandıktan birinci parti olarak çıkması halinde ilk kez iç istihbarat teşkilatı tarafından “kesin olarak aşırı sağcı” olarak sınıflandırılan bir parti bir eyalet seçiminde zaferini ilan etmiş olacak.

Ancak AfD’nin tek başına iktidara gelmesi, yalnızca oy oranına bağlı değil. Parti mutlak çoğunluğu sağlayamazsa seçimlerden birinci çıksa bile muhalefette kalabilir.

Saksonya-Anhalt’ta 2002 yılından bu yana iktidara gelen tüm eyalet başbakanları, Başbakan Friedrich Merz’in partisi CDU’dan çıktı. Eyalette halen CDU, Sosyal Demokrat Parti (SPD) ve Hür Demokrat Parti’den (FDP) oluşan koalisyon iktidarda. Eyalet parlamentosuna girmesi beklenen partilerin tamamı, AfD ile birlikte hükümet kurmayı reddettiğini belirtiyor. Bu nedenle hükümet kurma sürecinin zorlu geçmesi bekleniyor.

Nüfusu yaklaşık 2 milyon 100 bin olan Saksonya-Anhalt’ta genç nüfusun oranı oldukça düşük. Eyaletteki yaş ortalaması 2024 yılında 48,3 olarak kaydedildi. Almanya genelinde ise aynı yıl için ortalama yaş 44,9 olarak kayıtlara geçmişti. Yaklaşık 25 milyar avro kamu borcu bulunan Saksonya Anhalt, kişi başına düşen kamu borcu açısından Almanya’nın geniş yüzölçümlü eyaletleri arasında üst sıralarda yer alıyor. 65.5’lik istihdam oranı ise Almanya ortalamasının üzerinde bulunuyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: By Jo Kimmy, Contributor
title: Northern Thailand Communities March to Defend the Kok River from Mining Pollution
content:
Chiang Rai, Thailand — Hand-painted banners reading “Protect the Kok River” and “Bring Back Clean Water” waved above a crowd of farmers, fishers, scientists, and environmental activists as they walked along northern Thailand’s Kok River. For five days, hundreds of people marched 68 kilometers from Tha Ton in Chiang Mai province to Chiang Rai city, demanding action over toxic contamination flowing downstream from unregulated gold and critical minerals mines across the border in Myanmar (Burma).


As the march passed through riverside villages, participants stopped to discuss the issue with residents who have lived in harmony with the river for generations and whose livelihoods depend on it. In recent years, however, the river has become a source of worry rather than life.


Fishers described declining catches and fewer customers, as many people fear eating fish from the polluted river. Farmers worried about irrigating their fields, while mothers spoke about trying to keep their children away from swimming and playing in the water. For many, the demonstration was about more than pollution — it was a fight to protect a river that sustains entire communities.


The march concluded at Chiang Rai City Hall, where protesters delivered their demands after a planned meeting with Thailand’s prime minister was canceled. Although government representatives listened to the concerns of local residents, demonstrators left without clear commitments or a timeline for action. 


The contamination has become an increasingly urgent issue for communities in northern Thailand, where attention is turning toward the rapid expansion of critical minerals mining in neighboring Myanmar.


As demand for rare earth minerals grows worldwide, residents along the Kok River say they are paying the environmental price for an industry that operates beyond their control. According to the

Stimson Center

, nearly 800 unregulated mining sites along Mekong tributaries are potentially threatening waterways across the region. These sites pose a risk of contaminating rivers with toxic materials, including arsenic and cyanide, as well as heavy metals like mercury that can accumulate in river ecosystems.  


A River Under Threat

  


The Kok River begins in Myanmar’s Shan State before crossing into northern Thailand, where it flows through Chiang Rai province and eventually joins the Mekong River. Together, the Kok and Mekong rivers support some of the world’s richest freshwater ecosystems and have sustained communities for generations, providing water for drinking, farming, fishing, transportation, and cultural traditions.

 


Pictured: Kok River


For many residents, the river’s ecological transformation began after severe flooding struck northern Thailand in 2024. As communities worked to recover, local researchers started testing the river’s water and sediments.

In July 2025, they released findings

 showing increased concentrations of arsenic and other heavy metals in the Kok River downstream.


Since then, regular water sampling at multiple monitoring stations along the Kok, Sai, and Ruak rivers has continued to detect high levels of contaminants.


Although the long-term health impacts remain uncertain, exposure to arsenic and heavy metals is associated with an increased risk of serious illnesses, including cancer and damage to the liver, kidneys, and nervous system. Residents say the lack of clear information from authorities has only deepened their anxiety. Many first learned about the contamination through social media rather than official government announcements, and affected communities say they have received no support from the government.


While some residents have stopped fishing and avoid eating fish from the Kok River, many still depend on it for their daily survival. As concerns over contamination grow, access to safe food and clean water has become another form of inequality. For many, safer alternatives are too expensive or inaccessible, leaving them with little choice but to continue relying on the river.


“Before the flooding, we lived close to nature. We swam in the river and used it every day,” said Kru Nu, a teacher from a village on the banks of the Kok River. “After the flood, and then after the discovery of the toxic pollution, we realized that the river we had lived in harmony with for generations could be dangerous.”  


Voices From the Walk

  


For many participants, the Kok River is more than a waterway. It is an …

author: Act for freedom now!
title: HANDS OFF OUR COMRADES  Support for legal expenses of persecuted and incarcerated comrades for the Marfin case (Greece)
content:
https://www.firefund.net/legalexpensesformarfincase

Sixteen years later, the greek state is once again bringing the Marfin bank case to the forefront of media and repressive attention. The ‘New Democracy’ party (the ruling party) is attempting once again to criminalise the massive and highly confrontational protest that took place at 5 May of 2010 against the austerity measures designed to shift the burden of the economic crisis to the oppressed.

During this protest three workers who despite the general strike where forced to be at their workplace lost their lives. The trial has already concluded, resulting in the conviction of the bank’s CEO, the head of security and the branch manager. Yet, despite this there have been repeated attempts to frame comrades dragging them through sham trials where the state’s lies have been totally dismantled.

Sixteen years later, the government and its media is attempting to shift the pre-election agenda once again to the convenient target- the anarchist movement. Specifically, our comrades whose homes were raided, two of whom have been incarcerated and another one is waiting for extradition from the UK to appear before the interrogator . The ‘evidence’ presented in the media so far is reaching new levels of absurdity. From anonymous phone calls to which we have – unfortunately – become accustomed, we moved on to anonymous emails. AI software was deployed 16 years later to match photographs from… holidays showing similar clothing.Sixteen years later, the issues at stake remain the same. title: Stand and fight Calum Stuart
content:
Credit: Ivan Weiss


T

he day I interviewed Daniel York Loh, there was news of anti-immigration protests—some of which turned violent—erupting across Belfast, Northern Ireland. The BBC reported that people had been targeted simply for having “a different skin colour”.


In recent years, xenophobic and racist rhetoric has been on the rise in the UK. This has manifested alongside right-wing politicians and political parties (such as Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, and Tommy Robinson, a far-right activist) moving from fringe entities into mainstream influence. For Loh—an actor, writer, and filmmaker of Singaporean and British heritage who has been a vocal supporter of left-wing causes—these developments have been equal parts alarming and maddening.


Based in London, Loh has been working in the performing arts in both the UK and Asia for more than forty years. In that time, he’s become increasingly invested in working to improve Asian representation on stage and on screen. He was a founding member of BEATS (British East and Southeast Asian in Theatre and on Screen), a not-for-profit, volunteer-based advocacy group for British East and Southeast Asians working in theatre, film, or television. He’s also a member of the Race Equality Committee of Equity, the trade union for performers and creatives in the entertainment and performing arts industry. In 2016, he was one of twenty-one contributors to the anthology

The Good Immigrant

, reflecting on issues of race, immigration, identity, and Othering in the UK. A tenth anniversary issue of the book was launched this year.


More recently, Loh appeared in the true crime drama

I Fought The Law

, a four-part series following the determined struggle of Ann Ming—played by the award-winning British actor Sheridan Smith—a former nurse who campaigned for seventeen years to overturn the UK’s double jeopardy law after the murder of her daughter in 1989. Loh stars as Ming’s mixed-race husband, Charlie, in a story that examines grief and trauma, while not shying away from the racial politics of Britain in the 1980s and 1990s.


I’d like to start with

I Fought The Law

, which was based on a true story. It received rave reviews and you were nominated for an award at the 2026 Royal Television Society North East and the Borders Awards. What was it like taking on this role and playing a character based on a real person?


Daniel York Loh with Sheridan Smith in I Fought The Law. Credit: Anastasia A Arsentyeva


Charlie Ming, he was like me. He was mixed race but, essentially, very, very British. Very, very Middlesbrough [a town in North Yorkshire, England]. Ann Ming was kind of an advisor on the series, but [Charlie’s] not around anymore.


I Fought The Law

 was based on Ann Ming’s book [

For the Love of Julie

, published in 2009]. It was a real privilege to do it. It was such a good script and an amazing story. Sheridan Smith is an amazing actor and we had a great director [Erik Richter Strand]. I can’t speak highly enough of the whole thing, really.


I got the impression that it resonated with people because, right now, there’s a widespread sense of cynicism in many places. But in the series you have an ordinary person who’s taking on a massive system and prevailing.


I’m told the viewing figures were very high for the modern era. I think people were very taken with [the story]; it was a genuinely huge achievement. Ann Ming kept on going, she was very dogged, which I think people really admire… when you win in the end. If you’re very dogged and you don’t win, they kind of think you’re mad.


How do you feel the series dealt with the issue of racism?


There was a scene that flashed back to when Ann and Charlie were younger, and the racist neighbour comes around and there’s graffiti with racist slurs on the wall outside. And there were a few people online going, “Oh, typical ‘woke’ ITV.” But that’s in her book! It’s in Ann Ming’s book, and it was actually much worse. They suffered terrible racism when they first got together. I wanted that stuff in there. It’s important in social history and it resonates with what’s going on now.


There’s always people who want to blame migrants for anything and everything. If you put one foot out of line, your entire ‘community’—in inverted commas, because people don’t know each other a lot of the time—suffers. It reminds me of my own childhood. My childhood was basically [full of] racist abuse and my dad coming up to the school; the teachers …

title: Am autoritären Kipppunkt: „Law and Order“-Politik hat Konjunktur
content:
Dossier


„… In der Klimaforschung ist ein Kipppunkt ein Moment, an dem – laut Weltklimarat – „eine kritische Grenze“ erreicht wird, „jenseits derer sich ein System umorganisiert“, neue Prozesse sich verfestigen und negative Dynamiken sich beschleunigen. Dies lässt sich auch auf gesellschaftliche Kipppunkte übertragen. Kipppunkte entstehen nicht zufällig, sie sind das Ergebnis länger zurückliegender destruktiver Prozesse. Doch im Gegensatz zum Klima sind gesellschaftliche Prozesse nie unumkehrbar. Allerdings sind etablierte Diskurse, Strukturen und Normen oft nicht rückgängig zu machen. Sind autoritäre Kipppunkte überschritten, wird der Boden brüchig, auf dem plurale und demokratische Gesellschaften stehen…“

Kommentar von Daniel Mullis, Maximilian Pichl und Vanessa E. Thompson vom 16. Juni 2023 in der taz online


, siehe mehr daraus und dazu:


[Buch: »Erziehung zur Grausamkeit. Die Massenpsychologie des Neuen Faschismus«] Lehrjahre der Unmenschlichkeit: Faschismus als Prozess der Verrohung


„

Seit dreißig Jahren, in manchen Nationen sogar schon länger, erleben wir einen Aufstieg des rechten Populismus. Ultrarechte Parteien werden nicht nur stärker, viele radikalisieren sich auch nach und nach – oder sogar rasend schnell. Und eine entscheidende Rolle spielt dabei ein Kult der Härte, der die schräge Allianz aus Neuem Faschismus und Ultraliberalen fest zusammenhält.


Konnte man vor einigen Jahren noch vom aufkommenden »Rechtspopulismus« sprechen, wäre das heute in vielen Fällen eine Verharmlosung. Rechtsextremismus oder Neuer Faschismus trifft es da schon weit besser, bedenkt man, dass sich faschistische Bewegungen durch eine Reihe von Eigenschaften auszeichnen: Führerkult, paranoide Weltbilder, die permanent geschürt werden, ein Schwarz-Weiß-Denken, antagonistische Feindbilder, vor allem von Minderheiten, aber auch gegen vermeintliche innere Feinde. (…)


Faschismus ist, so gesehen, eher eine Stimmung, die einen nach und nach erfasst und überwältigt. Die Affekte von Gekränktheit, Angst, Neid, das Ressentiment und die Erlösungssehnsucht, sie alle sind ansteckend – und diese Ansteckung läuft nicht bloß von den Agitatoren zu den Anhängern, sondern wirkt kreuz und quer. Wie bei Synapsenverschaltungen werden die Verbindungen gestärkt, je intensiver sie benutzt werden. Emotionen, Tonfall und Phrasen werden übernommen, steigern sich zu Fanatismus.

Der Faschismus ist demnach weniger eine Ideologie als ein sozialer Prozess. Ansteckung ist kein Zufall, sie gedeiht in Milieus, in denen Gefühle zirkulieren wie ein Echo, das lauter zurückkehrt, als es ausgesendet wurde. Bis der Fanatiker am Ende als normal erscheint und der Normale als verdächtig.


Das trifft alles auf Parteien wie die MAGA-Bewegung der US-Republikaner zu, genauso auf die Alternative für Deutschland oder die Freiheitliche Partei in Österreich. Sie alle haben sich in den vergangenen Jahren in einem Prozess der Selbstradikalisierung markant verwandelt. Gewiss, Rechtspopulismus ist nicht dasselbe wie Faschismus, aber die Übergänge sind fließend. Wer als Rechtspopulist begann, kann als Faschist enden.


Und es geschah und geschieht dabei auch etwas Eigentümliches, das bis heute erst in Ansätzen verstanden wird: Die Radikalisierung der einen Partei wirkte als Aufschaukelung und Vorbildeffekt auf die anderen zurück. Das Resultat ist die Radikalisierung aller in einem längst globalen Resonanzraum. Simpel gesagt: Ohne Trump wäre die AfD wahrscheinlich gemäßigter, die FPÖ wäre ohne die AfD weniger radikal – und umgekehrt. (…)


Das ist das Neue an den neuen Rechtsradikalen: Sie können das Weiße Haus erobern, das mächtigste Amt der Welt, sie können beide Parlamentskammern kontrollieren, das höchste Gericht mehrheitlich mit Loyalisten besetzen und das Silicon Valley auf ihrer Seite haben – und betrachten sich noch immer als Widerstandskämpfer gegen eine »linke Hegemonie«. Dafür müssen sie nur Wohlerzogenheit, Respekt und die allgemein anerkannte Sittlichkeit als »links« ansehen. Der Spott über Behinderte wird dann geradezu zur gegenkulturellen Provokation. (…)


Der Rechtsradikale posiert als Widerstandskämpfer gegen den Mainstream – sogar dann, wenn er im mächtigsten Amt sitzt, das es in der Welt zu ergattern gibt. Der Rechtsradikale fühlt sich chronisch unterdrückt – meist durch die Tatsache, dass auch Menschen mit anderen Ansichten existieren – und zugleich mit einer höheren Macht im Bunde. (…)


Während sich die USA daranmachen, allmählich und rasant eine …

Der Bundesgerichtshof hat am 4. August 2026 (Az. StB 47/26) die Beschwerde von Lina E. gegen die im Juni vom OLG Dresden verhängten sechs Monate Beugehaft zurückgewiesen. Das OLG verhängte daraufhin Beugehaft. Der BGH hält in seiner Entscheidung von dieser Woche, die sechs Monate Beugehaft für rechtmäßig.


BGH: Kein Zeugnisverweigerungsrecht!


Das OLG wollte Lina zu „zu vier Überfällen der Vereinigung auf dem neonazistischen Spektrum zugeordnete Personen am 8. Januar 2019, 19. Oktober 2019, 14. Dezember 2019 und 15. Februar 2020, zu einem Diebstahl von Tatwerkzeugen am 13. Dezember 2019 sowie zur Auskundschaftung einer Zielperson im Juni 2020“ (Rz. 16, die Rz-Angaben beziehen sich auf das

PDF des BGH-Beschlusses

Allerdings berief sie sich vor dem OLG

§ 55 StPO

. Danach darf ein:e Zeug:in die Aussage verweigern, wenn sie/er sich selbst belasten könnte. Eine solche Gefahr der Selbstbelastung wollen weder OLG noch BGH anerkennen. Denn es gebe keine konkreten Anhaltspunkte dafür, dass Lina Gefahr liefe, durch eine Aussage, „relevante Verdachtsmomente für eine Beteiligung an einer anderen Tat“ einräumen zu müssen. „Bloße Vermutungen und spekulative Annahmen einer Verfolgungsgefahr genügen (…) nicht, um ein Auskunftsverweigerungsrecht (...) zu begründen“ (Rz.14), so der BGH.


BGH: keine Gefahr der Selbstbelastung


Das oberste deutsche Strafgericht kommt zu dem Schluss, Lina habe zwar „zum engeren Kreis der besonders engagierten und in zentraler Funktion tätigen Vereinigungsmitglieder gehört“ (Rz. 18). Die verschiedenen Überfälle seien zudem von wechselnden Gruppen begangen worden, und „die Struktur der Vereinigung sei) durch ein kollektives Selbstverständnis und eine Fungibilität (Anm: Austauschbarkeit) der Akteure gekennzeichnet“ (Rz. 18) gewesen.


Auch habe die Vereinigung über zahlreiche Mitglieder:innen sowie Unterstützer:innen verfügt. Deshalb lasse sich jedoch keineswegs aus einer Aussage über die bereits abgeurteilten Tatenauf eine Beteiligung an weiteren Taten schließen. Hinzu komme, dass die Ermittlungsbehörden ohnehin bereits umfassende Kenntnisse über die Vereinigung, die Rolle Linas und die abgeurteilten Taten hätten. Neue, sie selbst belastende Informationen seien von ihrer Aussage deshalb nicht zu erwarten.


BGH: zweimal Beugehaft, aber dennoch „nur“ sechs Monate Gesamtdauer


In der Berichterstattung ging bislang etwas unter, dass gegen Lina schon mit Beschluss vom 01.10.2025 vom Amtsgericht Dresden, im Rahmen eines von der Generalstaatsanwaltschaft Dresden geführten Ermittlungsverfahrens gegen Unbekannt, eine sechsmonatige Beugehaftanordnung angeordnet worden sind (Rz. 24). Es geht um einen Vorfall vom 08.01.2019, als ein

Kanalarbeiter in Leipzig-Connewitz

attackiert worden sein soll.


Das OLG entschied zwar, dass die Beugehaft letztlich nicht länger dauern dürfe als insgesamt sechs Monate, d.h. die Beugehaft vom Amtsgericht und jene vom OLG werden nicht nacheinander vollstreckt, sondern nach sechs Monaten gelten beide als erledigt.


Der BGH lässt jedoch erkennen, dass es durchaus möglich gewesen wäre, dies anders zu handhaben. Denn zwar dürfe „Beugehaft in demselben oder in einem anderen Verfahren, das dieselbe Tat zum Gegenstand hat, nicht wiederholt werden“ (Rz. 25). „Angesichts des Gewichts der (…) massiven Gewaltdelinquenz, ihrer Qualifikation als politisch motivierte linksextremistische Gewalttaten sowie der wahrscheinlichen genauen verfahrensrelevanten Kenntnisse der Beschwerdeführerin als Beteiligte an den Taten, (...) und als Angehörige der linksextremistischen Szene“ (Rz. 35), so der BGH, sei es verhältnismäßig sechs Monate Beugehaft anzuordnen.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: White House Reportedly Lobbied to Keep Accused Abuser Rep. Max Miller in Race
content:
One official suggested that Miller staying in the race seemed inevitable after he compared himself to Trump.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In the days before the Ohio deadline for candidates to be replaced, the White House waged a campaign to ensure that alleged abuser Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) stayed in his race for reelection, reportedly effectively telling Republicans to “back off” of criticisms of his candidacy.

Politico reported on Monday, citing three sources, that Donald Trump’s political team told Republicans in Ohio in the past week not to publicly criticize Miller. They reportedly said it would “complicate messaging” if Miller stayed in the race and they would then still have to back him — less concerned, seemingly, about the complications that now arise from their backing of a man accused of abusing his ex-wife and their daughter.

An Ohio Republican involved in the discussions told Politico that the White House “basically told us to back off … and let the voters decide.”

Ohio Republicans had reportedly discussed scheduling a meeting to replace Miller, but the White House advised against it, saying that he wasn’t going to drop out and that they wouldn’t be able to find a replacement.

One White House official even told Politico that Miller’s staying in the race seemed inevitable after the House representative compared his situation to the sexual assault allegations against Trump.

Miller has been insistent that he is staying in the race and on Monday surpassed the deadline to be replaced. He is running for reelection against Democrat and union ironworker Brian Poindexter.

Miller has been facing calls to resign ever since allegations came to light earlier this year that Miller once threw boiling water at his ex-wife, held a gun to her head, and fractured their 2-year-old daughter’s collarbone. The ex-wife in question is Emily Moreno, the daughter of Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno (Ohio).

Since the initial allegations, more disputes have come out, including that Miller recently refused to hand over his daughter’s beloved stuffed bunny for 48 hours, and that Miller accidentally shared pictures online of his daughter that some said could be considered child sex abuse material.

Republicans have largely been mum about Miller despite the allegations. Only a handful of Republicans have called for him to resign or withdraw, including his former father-in-law. Meanwhile, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) said last week that it’s not his “business” to be involved in “domestic events” with his members.

Many within the party believe that Miller will still win the election despite the allegations because Trump won the district by 11 points in 2024.

“It’s still winnable, it’s just going to be expensive,” one Republican told Politico.

Indeed, Politico polling recently found that most Trump supporters say they would still vote for a Republican candidate through numerous scandals. This includes if they were photographed wearing blackface (74 percent); accused of domestic violence (72 percent); or were accused of sexual assault (66 percent).

On Bolivia’s National Day of Solidarity with Victims of Sexual Assault and Against Sexual Violence Against Children and Adolescents, observed on 9 August, four Equality Now partner organisations across Latin America share what it means to work for justice, prevention and reparation.


9 August has its origins in Cochabamba, Bolivia, in 2006, when

Brisa de Angulo

, then a teenage survivor of sexual violence, organised a march to express solidarity with other survivors, remind them that they were not alone, and demand action from the authorities. That same year, the date was officially recognised in Cochabamba, and in 2007 it was established by law as a national commemoration in Bolivia.


Since then, organisations such as the

Breeze of Hope Foundation

 (Fundación una Brisa de Esperanza, FUBE), together with survivors and activists, have helped expand this initiative into a regional and international campaign promoting mobilisation, prevention, access to justice and reparation.


Equality Now works with partner organisations across Latin America and the Caribbean to end sexual violence and harmful practices, and to tackle discriminatory laws. Following the publication of our 2021 report

Failure to Protect: How Discriminatory Sexual Violence Laws and Practices Harm Women, Girls and Adolescents in the Americas

,

 we joined forces with a growing number of organisations across Latin America to establish the

Regional Access to Justice Network

. The Network aims to reform sexual violence laws and improve their implementation in order to ensure access to justice for survivors.


Addressing sexual violence against children and adolescents requires laws and public policies, but it also requires something more: transforming the narratives surrounding violence, reporting, survivors’ credibility and institutional responsibility. Shifting these narratives from suspicion and silence towards solidarity and justice is part of the work. Across the region, organisations are making this possible by supporting survivors, challenging harmful narratives and building collective responses.


For this occasion, we have brought together four partner voices from Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay and Colombia. Although they work in very different contexts, they share one conviction: no child or adolescent should have to face these forms of violence alone.


Paraguay – Alejandra Sosa, BECA


Since 2024, the

Educational and Community Support Foundation (BECA)

, together with partner organisations, has commemorated 9 August in Paraguay to urge both civil society and the State to recognise the significant gap in public policies providing reparation for survivors. In 2024 and 2025, they launched the campaign

What happens after a report is made? (in Spanish: ¿Qué sucede luego de la denuncia?)

, highlighting the lack of protection services available to children and adolescents experiencing sexual violence. This year, they also created spaces for dialogue and emotional support for survivors and their families.


Paraguay records nine reports of child sexual abuse every day. In this context, solidarity begins by recognising the courage it takes to break the silence and by supporting survivors without revictimising them, allowing each person the time they need. “Accessing justice and reparation requires a strong community to support you,” says Alejandra Sosa.


The change BECA is working towards follows two paths: strengthening public reparation policies, which are currently limited to an emerging programme run by the Ministry of Children and Adolescents that requires greater political commitment, and safeguarding Comprehensive Sexuality Education based on gender equality and human rights. Their experience demonstrates that mobilisation can bring about change.


Argentina – Julieta Santillán Juri, ANDHES


ANDHES (Lawyers of Northwest Argentina for Human Rights and Social Studies)

 works from a locally grounded perspective in north-west Argentina, where economic, territorial, gender and cultural inequalities shape people’s real opportunities to access justice. In 2023, together with …

author: Bridget Deacon
title: What young Kenyan men say when no one is watching
content:
A young Kenyan man recently sent this anonymous message to a chatbot late at night:


“Mbogi wanasema mimi si mwanaume nisipolala na huyo mama…

tangu lini mtu ashajiita mwanaume kwa sababu ya kulala na wanawake?”


(“My crew tells me I’m not a man if I don’t sleep with her.

Since when did sleeping with women make someone a man?”)


That single sentence may explain more about the state of masculinity in Kenya today than many formal reports ever could.


The message came through

Sema na Me

, an AI-enabled WhatsApp companion developed by

Shujaaz Inc.

 that allows young people to anonymously discuss relationships, sex, mental health and identity in Sheng without fear of judgement. Designed primarily as a safe and youth-friendly support platform, it has also become something else: an unusually candid window into the emotional realities many young Kenyan men rarely express publicly.


Between 30 October 2024 and 12 June 2026, young people exchanged more than 400,000 messages with the

Sema na Me

 WhatsApp chatbot with over 180,000 of them being about relationships, employment, mental health, identity and gender.


Our analysis draws from this anonymised platform data and qualitative conversation trends, providing an unusually large evidence base into the concerns young Kenyans voluntarily raise when they believe they are speaking in confidence. Further among users who self-reported demographic information while joining the platform, young men accounted for most of the gender-identified users, although an increasing share of users in 2026 chose not to disclose gender.


Across Kenya today, young men are navigating a rapidly changing social and economic reality with very few spaces to process what it means.

Expectations around manhood remain stubbornly fixed

: provide financially, suppress vulnerability, prove masculinity constantly and maintain control. Yet the economic and social conditions required to fulfil those expectations are shifting rapidly.


Many young men are struggling quietly in the gap between those two realities.


This is not simply anecdotal. Across the

Sema na Me

 platform, conversations about employment, financial pressure, relationships and emotional wellbeing consistently rank among the most common discussion themes raised by young users. Many of these conversations reveal the same underlying tension: expectations of masculinity remain high while opportunities to fulfil them are becoming increasingly uncertain.


This tension is unfolding at a moment of wider uncertainty for young Kenyans.

High unemployment, rising living costs and the social aftershocks of recent youth-led protests have intensified questions around identity, dignity and belonging

. Much of that negotiation is now happening online, where algorithm-driven content increasingly shapes how young men understand power, relationships and masculinity.


This reflects a broader trend. According to the

International Labour Organization

, young people continue to face disproportionate challenges entering and remaining in decent work


At the same time,

Kenya recorded one of its deadliest years for women in 2024

, with reports of femicide and gender-based violence increasing sharply according to rights groups and media investigations.

Young Kenyan men also continue to die by suicide at significantly higher rates than young women

, often in silence and with little access to support.

The World Health Organization

 has in its reports consistently highlighted that men account for a disproportionate share of suicide deaths globally.


These crises are often discussed separately. Increasingly, they should not be.


Analysis of more than 2.3 million anonymous conversations suggests these concerns are neither isolated nor rare. Anonymous youth engagement platforms such as Sema na Me provide one of the clearest windows into how young people discuss masculinity when they believe they will not be judged. The anonymity matters. Users know they are not speaking to a parent, teacher, politician or religious authority. They are speaking into a neutral and non-judgmental space that responds in their own language and on platforms they already use daily.


As a result, conversations that might otherwise remain hidden begin to surface.
